questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Underwriting Platform for a Commercial Insurer (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Commercial Insurance wants to modernize how it triages and prices incoming commercial property and casualty submissions. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with underwriting leadership.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals Meridian's actual goal is cutting turnaround time for standard submissions from five days to one day with the same underwriter headcount — not expanding into new lines of business.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around transformation, arguing this initiative should be marketed as creating an entirely new underwriting capability rather than speeding up an existing one.
Frame it around cost reduction exclusively, since headcount is unchanged and payroll is the only budget lever leadership will actually fund.
Skip framing around any specific value pillar; a working system justifies itself regardless of what discovery uncovered.
Frame it around efficiency, and build success metrics around cycle time and throughput per underwriter rather than novel capability.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (faster turnaround, same headcount) is a throughput/efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. A, B, and C either misname the pillar or skip the framing that keeps the project aligned to what discovery actually found.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Underwriting Platform for a Commercial Insurer (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Commercial Insurance wants to modernize how it triages and prices incoming commercial property and casualty submissions. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with underwriting leadership.
questions.prompt: The right sequence of underwriting steps varies by submission type, industry class, prior loss history, and information discovered along the way.

choices.text: An agentic pattern, since the sequence of steps varies by case and depends on findings discovered along the way rather than one predetermined path.
A fixed workflow, since commercial underwriting has an established process every submission should follow identically regardless of what's discovered.
An augmented LLM pattern, since a single retrieval-enhanced call is enough to handle any underwriting workflow, however varied.
Whichever pattern the team can implement fastest, since the four patterns are functionally interchangeable for this kind of task.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by case and depend on intermediate findings are the defining case for an agentic pattern. B assumes a predictability the scenario explicitly lacks; C undersells the orchestration actually needed; D ignores that the patterns have real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Underwriting Platform for a Commercial Insurer (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Commercial Insurance wants to modernize how it triages and prices incoming commercial property and casualty submissions. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with underwriting leadership.
questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to specialized subagents (submission intake, risk scoring, actuarial pricing lookup, underwriting-decision recommendation).

choices.text: Let each subagent pass results directly to whichever subagent needs them next, cutting out the coordinator hop to reduce turnaround time and simplify the message path.
Merge all four responsibilities into a single subagent so there's no coordination overhead or handoffs to manage at all.
Let subagents communicate directly, but log the peer-to-peer traffic in a structured audit trail so it can be reviewed later if needed.
Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. A and C sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; B discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents in the first place.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Underwriting Platform for a Commercial Insurer (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Commercial Insurance wants to modernize how it triages and prices incoming commercial property and casualty submissions. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with underwriting leadership.
questions.prompt: Every subagent completes its assigned work correctly, but the coordinator's decomposition assigned only standard property submissions to the pipeline — excess and umbrella liability submissions are never routed to any subagent and silently fall through.

choices.text: Fix the coordinator's decomposition to explicitly cover every submission category, including excess and umbrella liability, instead of tuning subagents that already work.
Add a prompt instruction telling each subagent to flag any submission type it doesn't recognize, so routing gaps surface downstream instead of failing silently.
Give the existing subagents broader tool access so any one of them could, in principle, handle a submission type it wasn't originally scoped for.
Add a fifth subagent dedicated to edge-case submissions, without changing how the coordinator's routing logic decides what counts as an edge case in the first place, leaving the same gap.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while whole submission categories are never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. B, C, and D all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap.

Efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, and performance SLAs are examples of such pillars that should drive both architecture and metrics.
Business value pillars are a sales and marketing concern, not something that belongs in an architectural conversation with leadership.

choices.text: Ignore the sentiment entirely, since job-security concerns aren't a technical requirement the architecture needs to satisfy.
Proceed with the technical design as planned and let change management handle the sentiment separately, with no architectural input at all.
Treat it as a real implicit constraint alongside the explicit technical requirements — it will shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter most.
Recommend against the project entirely on the strength of this sentiment alone, without weighing it at all against the turnaround-time and same-headcount case that originally motivated pursuing it.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG and Model Selection for a Manufacturing Predictive-Maintenance Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Ironclad Manufacturing wants Claude to help maintenance technicians diagnose equipment issues using both general reasoning and retrieval over equipment manuals, sensor telemetry logs, and historical maintenance records. questions.prompt: Most technician questions are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step diagnostic reasoning across sensor history and manuals, and a small fraction are simple lookups (e.g., part numbers).

choices.text: Use one fixed model tier for every question regardless of complexity, so the routing logic stays as simple as possible to build and maintain, even though the mix of questions ranges from simple lookups to deep diagnostic reasoning.
Route based on task difficulty — fast tier for simple lookups, balanced tier for typical questions, higher-capability tier for deep diagnostic cases.

Treat more tools as always improving flexibility, and actively encourage adding further unrelated capabilities.
Increase the subagent's context window, on the theory that a bigger window offsets a larger, less-structured tool list.
Remove or relocate the unrelated tools, since this capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability.

Run routing and customs-check as independent, parallel subagent calls once procurement completes.
Say true parallelization isn't possible once a coordinator delegates to specialized subagents.
Merge routing and customs-check into one subagent so the sequencing question never has to be answered.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no shared dependency can run in parallel once their prerequisite (procurement) completes, cutting latency without sacrificing correctness. A and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most attorney queries are moderately complex research questions; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many cases, and a small fraction are simple citation lookups.

choices.text: Route by difficulty — a fast tier for citation lookups, a balanced tier for typical research, and a higher-capability tier with extended thinking for deep multi-case reasoning.
Always use the highest-capability tier, to guarantee quality on every single question regardless of its actual difficulty.
Use one fixed model tier for every question, regardless of whether it's a lookup or a multi-case synthesis.
Always use the fastest, cheapest tier, accepting the quality loss on the deep multi-case questions.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex research questions. B and D ignore fit-to-task; C sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (jurisdiction rules, citation style, formatting requirements) followed by retrieved case excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Say prompt ordering doesn't affect cost or latency for a retrieval-heavy legal research workload.
Place the stable system prompt first with caching enabled, and the varying retrieved excerpts after it.
Put the retrieved excerpts before the system prompt, since they're the content most relevant to the specific attorney query.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt on each turn.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form judicial opinions with short structured data (a table of statute citations and effective dates).

choices.text: Use one chunking strategy tuned for long-form opinions and apply it to the short structured statute table too.
Match chunking and indexing strategy to each data shape, since one strategy tuned for opinions degrades retrieval for structured records.
Exclude the structured statute-citation table from retrieval entirely, keeping only long-form opinions indexed.
Use the largest possible chunk size everywhere, to avoid maintaining two separate chunking strategies.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and D ignore this mismatch; C discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorney queries range from exact lookups ("cite for Smith v. Jones") to conceptual questions ("how has the reasonable-reliance standard evolved across circuits").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search, ignoring the structured citation metadata, for both exact lookups and conceptual questions.
Use only structured or metadata filtering, for both exact citation lookups and open-ended conceptual questions.
Match retrieval to query pattern: metadata filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where both matter.
Treat query pattern as irrelevant to which retrieval approach is the right fit for a given attorney question.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and B force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorneys need citations that reliably map each legal claim to a specific case and pincite, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Require structured output pairing each claim with its case, reporter citation, and pincite, so mapping survives synthesis.
Ask the model, in prose only, to "always cite sources," with no schema or field structure behind the instruction.
Add citations after drafting, by searching afterward for a plausible case to attach to each already-written claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted cases at the end, without tying any specific claim to a specific source.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. B, C, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)

questions.prompt: Two retrieved cases disagree on how a particular statute of limitations is tolled — likely because they're from different circuits with different precedent.

choices.text: Average the two circuits' tolling positions together and present a single blended rule to the attorney.
Omit the tolling analysis from the answer entirely, since the two retrieved cases disagree with each other.
Always prefer whichever of the two conflicting cases the retrieval system happened to return first.
Present both positions explicitly, attributed to their respective circuits, rather than blending or silently picking one.

questions.explanation: Presenting both positions with attribution preserves the actual information for the attorney rather than resolving a genuine jurisdictional conflict arbitrarily. A, B, and C all discard or obscure a real disagreement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)

choices.text: Repeat the "always output valid JSON" instruction more emphatically, assuming the model's structured output is deterministic once phrased right.
Increase max_tokens, on the theory that more room fixes a preamble the model keeps generating before the JSON.
Use tool-use or schema-constrained output so structure is enforced by the API mechanism, not requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip any leading text that appears before the first curly brace.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and D are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; B doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)

questions.prompt: The platform needs to connect to a proprietary internal brief bank, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond just this research platform.

Paste the entire proprietary brief bank into every prompt that might need to reference it.
Build an MCP server exposing brief-bank operations as tools/resources, reusable across the internal tools.
Require each internal tool that needs the brief bank to reimplement its own separate integration and authentication layer independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. A, B, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.prompt: The team debates between exposing the full case-law catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

Treat context cost as roughly the same either way, since loading the full catalog and querying it on demand end up costing about the same per query.
Never expose the catalog to the agent in any form, forcing attorneys to search it manually outside Claude.
Use progressive discovery, querying a catalog resource as needed, which scales better as the corpus grows.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. A and B ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; C removes needed capability entirely.

questions.prompt: An attorney asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several retrieved opinions before concluding on a multi-factor test.

Use zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance, since it performs equally well on any multi-document synthesis task.
Treat chain-of-thought prompting as useful only for coding tasks, not for legal multi-factor analysis.
Say the model can't reason across multiple documents no matter which prompting approach is used.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning across a multi-factor test. B, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

Use modular, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — distinct from caching's cost/latency role or Skills' capability packaging.

Say standardization across features isn't something prompt design can achieve at all.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. A reintroduces duplication; C conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.

Trust the fluent, well-cited-looking output as sufficient evidence that the holding was already validated.
Say this is purely a model limitation with no architectural mitigation available at all.
Increase the output's length, on the theory that more room to elaborate reduces misstatement risk.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted holdings against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. B is the failure mode itself; D doesn't address correctness; C incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

Treat SLAs as a stakeholder-communication topic with no bearing on the technical tier-selection decision.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, B, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform (Questions 16–30)

Never upgrade the model again once an initial version has been chosen for production.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since an improved benchmark score guarantees a production improvement.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. B and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; C over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

Say output length has no practical limit, regardless of how much retrieved content the input already uses.
Balance retrieved-content volume against room for a detailed answer, since input and output share one context budget.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and C all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only forecast accuracy against actuals and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety/guardrail behavior.

choices.text: Treat forecast accuracy alone as sufficient, since it's the copilot's stated primary purpose.
Treat latency and cost as pure operations concerns, unrelated to how evaluation itself is designed.
Treat safety and guardrail metrics as relevant only for heavily regulated industries like finance or healthcare, not an internal sales copilot.
Define accuracy, latency, cost, and safety as first-class metrics, since forecasting well isn't enough on its own.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it forecasts well. A, B, and C each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. Replace the automated checks entirely with human review, dropping automation from the eval suite altogether.
Use mixed methods — automated eval for scale, manager judgment for nuanced calls, adversarial testing for safety paths.
Expand the labeled historical dataset indefinitely, treating that as the sole lever for improving evaluation.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and D each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

Change the prompt version and the underlying model tier at the same time, to try to maximize the potential improvement in one pass.
Skip testing altogether, on the assumption that prompt changes are inherently low-risk.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, isolating that one variable.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; C dismisses a real risk without evidence.

Treat this as a model-tier mismatch requiring a switch to a different, presumably more capable tier, regardless of what the investigation actually found.
Treat it as a prompt or generation issue — inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved data — needing prompt or output-validation fixes.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and C misdiagnose the layer at fault; B avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-sync event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, B, and D would not specifically correlate with a CRM data-sync refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. choices.text: Optimize cost, latency, and accuracy each independently, in isolation from the other two.
Always maximize accuracy first, regardless of what it costs or how much latency it adds.
Optimize cost, latency, and accuracy jointly against the SLA and budget, instead of maximizing any one alone.
Say this tradeoff can't be measured at all with the data currently available, only guessed at from prior experience.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and B optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

Treat aggregate accuracy as automatically representative of performance in every single region and every deal-size bucket without exception.
Refuse to reduce manager review at all, regardless of what a segment-level analysis might show.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by region and deal size before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prompt version improves narrative-quality ratings, but the team has not checked whether it also changed the rate of overconfident forecasts on genuinely volatile deals that should be flagged as uncertain.

choices.text: Check the uncertainty-flagging rate on volatile deals, since a narrative-quality gain could hide more overconfidence there.
Treat the narrative-quality rating alone as a sufficient signal that the new prompt is safe to ship.
Say overconfidence behavior on volatile deals isn't something an evaluation can actually measure.
Ship the new prompt version to all reps and monitor informally afterward instead of testing for this specific failure mode beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated narrative-quality improvement could mask a worsened overconfidence failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. B and D ship without adequate testing; C incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of forecasts are numerically accurate but rated as unhelpful by sales managers in feedback surveys.

choices.text: Investigate a dimension beyond accuracy, like actionability or relevance to the manager's own pipeline.
Assume the accuracy metric itself must be broken, and discard it from the eval suite entirely.
Increase the model's capability tier across the board, on the assumption that higher capability always raises perceived helpfulness too.
Ignore the manager feedback survey scores, since the accuracy metric alone is already validated by past quarters.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but unhelpful" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (actionability, explanation quality) rather than a broken accuracy metric. B and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; C assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends the full deal history plus a large static sales-methodology reference on every turn of multi-turn conversations with reps.

choices.text: Say there's no optimization opportunity here at all, since sending the full deal history on every single turn is always strictly required.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever considered for reducing per-turn token cost.
Remove the sales-methodology reference entirely, dropping it from every turn to save tokens.
Cache the static methodology reference and trim older turns to cut redundant token cost.

questions.explanation: Caching the static methodology reference and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. A denies an obvious lever; C removes needed content; B is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. It's been in production for six months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running A/B tests on prompt/model changes.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production copilot, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Treat raw logging at full volume, with every prompt and response captured verbatim, as itself a sufficient observability strategy.
Reduce logging volume to save on storage cost, without validating whether the reduced set still captures failure patterns.
Say observability needs no structure at all, as long as the raw data is retained somewhere.
Redesign observability toward structured, sampled signals with tagged failure categories.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and C accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a specific forecast-quality regression was caused by a recent prompt change, a recent model version change, or a CRM schema change — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: Assume the most recently shipped change is always the one responsible for the regression.
Isolate and re-test each of the three changes independently, since attribution requires exactly that discipline.
Say attribution becomes impossible once more than one change has shipped in the same week.
Revert all three changes at once immediately without investigating which one, if any of them, actually caused the regression.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and D guess without evidence; C gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a forecast-narrative output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: Say the model itself is malfunctioning and should be scheduled for a full retraining cycle based on these intermittent evaluation failures.
Make the fixed reference string longer, so the exact-match check has more text to compare against.
Replace the exact-match eval with a content/structure check, since output varies run to run even at a fixed temperature and won't suit exact matching.
Increase the temperature setting, on the theory that it will fix the eval's intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; B doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered copilot at Northwind Analytics helps sales reps and managers forecast pipeline and deal close probability. choices.text: Say a single number is always achievable and sufficient for evaluating any production system.
Use forecast accuracy alone as the single number, since it matches the copilot's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric to leadership under any circumstances, insisting only on a full multi-page breakdown.
Offer a single aggregate metric as a top-line indicator, paired with segment-level detail so it can't mask a failing area.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and B oversimplify to a single lossy number; C refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industries, a global manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-line quality-inspection assistant across plants in multiple countries, alongside internal Claude Code enablement for its distributed engineering teams. You are responsible for governance, phased global rollout, lifecycle management, and developer enablement.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data residency, retention, and access-logging design for plant-floor quality data in the final weeks before the first regional rollout, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: Say this sequencing carries no risk, since compliance details can always be bolted on right before launch.
Say compliance only affects legal paperwork, with no bearing on the system's actual architecture.
Say cross-border residency and access-control requirements can force structural changes costlier to retrofit than to design in up front.
Assume a single global data-handling policy is guaranteed to satisfy every plant's local regulatory regime across every country of operation.

questions.explanation: Cross-border data residency, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and B understate real architectural impact; D wrongly assumes one policy fits every regime.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industries, a global manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-line quality-inspection assistant across plants in multiple countries, alongside internal Claude Code enablement for its distributed engineering teams. You are responsible for governance, phased global rollout, lifecycle management, and developer enablement.
questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single output the quality-inspection system produces across all plants, framing it as the safest governance posture for a global rollout.

choices.text: Say maximal human review on every output is always the correct default posture for manufacturing AI.
Say human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model, making review counterproductive everywhere.
Target human-in-the-loop at high error-cost or judgment-requiring calls, since blanket review on every output defeats the system's value.
Say this blanket-review approach is required by every relevant regulatory regime that could plausibly apply to this global rollout, regardless of other considerations.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically, like borderline defect calls. A and B overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; D makes an unsupported blanket regulatory claim.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)

You are responsible for governance, phased global rollout, lifecycle management, and developer enablement.
questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from free-text inspector notes, and inconsistent output — as part of its design across every plant.

choices.text: Design mitigations for each known failure mode up front — grounding for hallucination, isolation for injection, validation for consistency.
Address these risks only if and when they're actually observed happening in production first.
Say a single generic guardrail addresses hallucination, injection, and inconsistency equally well.
Say these risks are exclusive to consumer-facing products built for the public, not to an internal manufacturing tool used by trained staff.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. B defers to a reactive posture; C assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; D is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industries, a global manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-line quality-inspection assistant across plants in multiple countries, alongside internal Claude Code enablement for its distributed engineering teams. questions.prompt: The plant-safety team asks whether the system's defect-flagging decisions could produce inconsistent outcomes across different plants with different equipment vintages and lighting conditions.

choices.text: Say this isn't an architectural concern at all, and belongs entirely to legal review after launch.
Say disparate outcomes across plants are impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
Evaluate whether eval data reflects the range of plant conditions and measure for disparate performance rather than assume it's absent.
Say this concern only applies to a system making final automated shutdown decisions on its own, not one that merely assists a human inspector.

questions.explanation: Consistency and fairness across deployment contexts are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness across plant conditions, disparate-performance checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; B and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: Engineering teams across Ferrotech's plants have inconsistent Claude Code usage — some plants have team conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access to plant systems varies by machine.

choices.text: Restrict Claude Code usage globally to a single designated engineer, to reduce configuration variance.
Standardize the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP configuration at the organization level, so behavior doesn't depend on local setup.
Have each plant's engineers individually troubleshoot their own local configuration as issues come up.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable, permanent cost of running a coordinated rollout across so many plants and countries.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the organization level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. C and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; A sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the organization.

questions.prompt: The team wants Claude Code-generated code changes to plant-control-adjacent software to go through the same review rigor as any other change to a safety-relevant system.

Keep standard SDLC practices in place — review, testing, version control — since AI assistance doesn't reduce required rigor.
Apply only a light spot-check to AI-generated code, skipping the review a human-written change would get.
Lower review requirements specifically for AI-generated code relative to equivalent human-written changes to the same system.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially for safety-relevant systems. A, C, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for this context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industries, a global manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-line quality-inspection assistant across plants in multiple countries, alongside internal Claude Code enablement for its distributed engineering teams. questions.prompt: A production incident at one plant traces back to a Claude Code-generated change to the inspection-data pipeline. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated code logic or in how the plant's surrounding system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug lives in the generated code without validating that assumption against the surrounding integration.
Disable Claude Code across every plant globally following this one incident.
Roll back every recent Claude Code-assisted change at every plant worldwide, regardless of whether it's even related to this incident.
Triage it the way any incident is triaged — isolate integration versus code/model failure using traces and logs.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and C skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industries, a global manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-line quality-inspection assistant across plants in multiple countries, alongside internal Claude Code enablement for its distributed engineering teams. Package the recurring report as a Skill for consistent reuse; leave the one-off investigation unstructured.
Build both the recurring report and the one-off sensor investigation as dedicated MCP servers, regardless of their actual reuse profile.
Say recurring workflows and one-off explorations should always be built the same way.

A under-serves the recurring task; C over-engineers the one-off task; D ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

questions.prompt: Ferrotech's compliance team wants documented evidence of who accessed what plant-floor quality data through the system and when, across every regional deployment.

choices.text: Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity and monitoring requirements.
Treat access logging as optional, as long as the system already has a structured, role-based permission scheme configured.
Say audit logging can be added later, with no real impact on the architecture built up to that point.
Log only failed access attempts, leaving every successful access to plant-floor data completely unrecorded and unreviewable.

Skip stakeholder communication entirely until the system is fully rolled out to every plant.
Tailor architectural communication to each audience, framing tradeoffs in terms plant operations and legal/compliance can evaluate.
Send identical technical documentation to every audience across every region, to save time preparing separate materials for each group.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by plant operations, legal/compliance, and engineering alike. A, B, and D each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)

Re-engage discovery for the affected region's scope, communicate the tradeoff, and adjust design and timeline.
Incorporate the regulatory change silently, without telling stakeholders what it changes.
Restart the entire global rollout from scratch across every plant and region, regardless of how narrow the regulation's actual scope is.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected region's scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally-driven requirements shift. A and C mishandle a real change; D disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Ferrotech Industries, a global manufacturer, is rolling out a Claude-powered production-line quality-inspection assistant across plants in multiple countries, alongside internal Claude Code enablement for its distributed engineering teams. Treat this as correct — monitoring and iteration become entirely the local operations team's responsibility once handoff is complete.
Treat lifecycle responsibility as ending once the rollout contract is signed.
Say monitoring is only necessary if a major incident actually occurs at a given plant.

Say documenting the reasoning behind each value is unnecessary overhead in a multi-region rollout.
Capture the "why" behind key decisions — compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning — so a future team can safely extend the system.
Say only the original architect should ever be allowed to modify the system, making documentation moot.

questions.explanation: Capturing the "why" (regional compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning) alongside the "what" is what lets a future team safely extend or modify the system at any plant. A, B, and D all leave that reasoning undocumented and effectively lost.

questions.prompt: Plant engineering teams want Claude Code to help with routine tasks (drafting maintenance documentation, exploring an unfamiliar legacy control module) but are unsure where it actually saves meaningful time versus adding review overhead.

choices.text: Assume AI-assisted tooling always saves meaningful time on every task category by default.
Ban Claude Code for all documentation tasks outright, without evaluating where it actually helps.
Mandate Claude Code usage for every single task across every plant, regardless of any measured benefit or engineer feedback about actual time saved.
Evaluate task categories for genuine friction reduction versus overhead that may exceed the time saved.

questions.explanation: Evaluating specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead gives an evidence-based answer instead of assuming a blanket benefit either way. A and C over-assume benefit; B forecloses potential benefit without evaluation.

Document the triage process — how to tell integration-layer failures from model-output failures — as shared operational knowledge.
Restrict all debugging of Claude Code integration failures to one designated global engineer.
Say the issue can only be resolved by switching to an entirely different tool.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Harrow & Vance LLP, a mid-size litigation firm, is building an internal e-discovery platform to handle document classification, privilege review, custodian communication analysis, and production packaging for large litigation matters. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the firm's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the firm's actual goal is processing 3x the current document volume per matter with the same review-team headcount, while preserving the same defensibility standard — not new capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around transformation, since stakeholders generally expect new capability from any AI investment regardless of what discovery found.
Frame the architecture around cost reduction exclusively, treating the headcount-neutral volume target as a budget line item to report upward each quarter.
Skip framing around a specific value pillar, since a system that technically works should speak for itself once it ships to the review team.
Frame the architecture around efficiency, building success metrics around review throughput per attorney-hour while holding the existing defensibility standard fixed and auditable.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (3x volume, same headcount, same defensibility standard) is a throughput/efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. A, B, and C either misname the pillar or skip the framing that keeps the project aligned to what discovery actually found.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)

questions.prompt: Document classification, privilege review, and production each require different steps depending on document type, privilege signals surfaced along the way, and custodian context discovered mid-review.

choices.text: A fixed workflow, since e-discovery follows a well-established legal process whose steps don't need to adapt to what review turns up midstream.
An augmented LLM pattern, since one enhanced call with retrieval of privilege rules is sufficient to handle any document regardless of custodian context.
An agentic pattern, since the right next step varies by document type and depends on findings surfaced partway through the review.
Whichever pattern implements fastest this quarter, since the four orchestration patterns produce functionally interchangeable outcomes for a workflow this thoroughly validated.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by document and depend on intermediate findings are the defining case for an agentic pattern. A assumes a predictability the scenario explicitly lacks; B undersells the orchestration actually needed; D ignores that the patterns have real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Harrow & Vance LLP, a mid-size litigation firm, is building an internal e-discovery platform to handle document classification, privilege review, custodian communication analysis, and production packaging for large litigation matters. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the firm's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to specialized subagents (document classification, privilege detection, redaction, production formatting).

choices.text: Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow across the pipeline.
Let subagents communicate directly with each other, but log the traffic centrally afterward so the coordinator can review what was exchanged.
Merge all four responsibilities into a single subagent, since coordination overhead outweighs keeping classification, privilege, redaction, and formatting separate.
Let each subagent hand its output directly to whichever subagent needs it next, minimizing hops through the coordinator layer.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. B and D sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; C discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents in the first place.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)

questions.prompt: Every subagent completes its assigned work correctly, but the coordinator's decomposition routes only email-format documents into the pipeline — scanned PDFs and chat-export logs are never routed to any subagent and silently fall through, missing production.

choices.text: Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers every document source type, including scanned PDFs and chat exports.
Add a prompt instruction telling each subagent to flag any document type it doesn't recognize as unrouted, then queue it for a nightly reconciliation review.
Give the existing subagents broader tool access so they can pull in document types the coordinator never actually sends them.
Add a fifth subagent dedicated to handling edge-case document types the coordinator currently drops on the floor.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while whole document-source categories are never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. B, C, and D all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap.

questions.scenario_context: Harrow & Vance LLP, a mid-size litigation firm, is building an internal e-discovery platform to handle document classification, privilege review, custodian communication analysis, and production packaging for large litigation matters. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the firm's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The design must align technical architecture to a specific business value pillar the firm actually cares about, distinct from a generic "we added AI" narrative.

choices.text: Any AI system inherently demonstrates transformation to stakeholders, so no additional value-pillar framing is required before this launch, regardless of what discovery found.
Business value pillars are a business-development concern for the client relationship team, not something the technical architecture itself needs to reflect.
Efficiency, risk-reduction/defensibility, cost-per-gigabyte, and cycle-time-to-production are pillar examples; the chosen one should drive the architecture and its metrics.
The pillar should be picked after the matter closes, based on whichever benefit turns out easiest to measure in hindsight.

questions.explanation: Business value pillars (efficiency, defensibility, cost-per-gigabyte, cycle time) give both the architecture and its metrics a clear anchor. A, B, and D all skip or defer this framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Harrow & Vance LLP, a mid-size litigation firm, is building an internal e-discovery platform to handle document classification, privilege review, custodian communication analysis, and production packaging for large litigation matters. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with the firm's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The firm's associates and paralegals are skeptical of automation and worried about reduced review hours; discovery interviews surface this repeatedly.

choices.text: Ignore the sentiment since staff comfort with automation isn't a technical requirement the architecture needs to accommodate before launch.
Treat it as a real implicit constraint alongside the explicit technical requirements — it shapes adoption, rollout sequencing, and where checkpoints matter most.
Proceed with the technical design as planned and let change management handle staff sentiment separately, with no architectural input into rollout sequencing at all, even later.
Recommend against the project entirely, since staff skepticism surfacing repeatedly this early is a strong enough signal on its own that the initiative will fail.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment is a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter — it's discovery input, not noise to ignore. A and C treat it as out of scope; D overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing it against the technical case.

questions.prompt: A partner asks why the privilege-detection subagent uses a higher-capability, higher-cost model tier than the document-classification subagent.

choices.text: Use the same model tier everywhere for simplicity, since tier differences are usually more about habit than actual task difficulty.
Explain the tradeoff explicitly: privilege determinations carry high legal risk and need deeper reasoning that justifies the added cost and latency involved.
Tell the partner "higher tier because it's more important" and move on, since that captures the gist without needing further technical detail.
Avoid explaining tier differences to partners at all, since the reasoning behind model selection is an implementation detail non-technical stakeholders won't find useful.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. A and C withhold the reasoning stakeholders need; D removes a deliberate, justified difference for false simplicity.

questions.prompt: The architecture's current design produces a final production recommendation with no mechanism to learn from attorney overrides of privilege or relevance calls over time.

choices.text: Add a feedback loop that captures attorney overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component, so the system keeps improving after deployment.
Accept the current design as-is, since a system that already reflects best practice at launch doesn't need a mechanism for learning from later corrections.
Treat feedback loops as a data science concern to raise with the analytics team after launch, unrelated to the architecture itself.
Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase, since nothing about the current design needs to account for it right now.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures attorney overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve after deployment, per the input→processing→output→feedback loop framing. B, C, and D all treat a first-class architectural component as optional or someone else's problem.

questions.prompt: A litigation support team wants a single enhanced LLM call — with retrieval of privilege-rule guidance — to answer straightforward attorney questions about privilege categories, without any multi-step autonomous orchestration.

choices.text: This requires a fixed workflow with a structured five-step sequence, since privilege-category questions always follow the same predictable steps.
This cannot be built with Claude at all, since anything involving retrieval implies an agentic architecture Claude doesn't support for simple lookups.
An augmented LLM pattern — a single call enhanced with retrieval — fits this simpler augmentation need without the overhead of agentic orchestration.
This calls for a full multi-agent architecture regardless of task simplicity, since privilege questions always warrant the most capable pattern available.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with retrieval, without multi-step autonomous orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern is for. A and D over-engineer a simple augmentation need; B is factually wrong.

questions.prompt: The document-classification subagent's toolset has grown to include tools for billing entry and calendar scheduling that are unrelated to document classification.

choices.text: This has no architectural downside as long as the subagent's prompt is well-written and its inputs are validated before each tool call.
More tools always improve a subagent's flexibility and should be encouraged, since a broader toolset only expands what a well-prompted subagent handles.
The fix is to increase the subagent's context window, so it has more room to reason about which tool actually applies here.
This capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability; the unrelated billing and calendar tools should be removed or relocated to a more appropriate subagent.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows — the fix is removing or relocating them, not just adding input checks around the existing sprawl. A and B ignore this real degradation; C doesn't address selection reliability at all.

questions.prompt: The coordinator currently processes each document sequentially through classification, privilege detection, relevance scoring, and redaction, even though privilege detection and relevance scoring have no dependency on each other's output.

choices.text: Run privilege detection and relevance scoring as independent, parallel subagent calls once classification completes, instead of processing every stage sequentially.
Sequential processing of every stage is required to preserve chain-of-custody defensibility for the eventual production package handed to opposing counsel and the court.
Parallelization isn't possible within a coordinator/subagent architecture, since subagents can only run one at a time by design.
Combine privilege detection and relevance scoring into a single subagent so the sequencing question doesn't need to be answered.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (classification) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. B and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

questions.prompt: General counsel asks how the end-to-end architecture should be described at a high level for a steering committee unfamiliar with the technical details.

choices.text: Present only the model names and per-document token costs involved, since that's the financial detail a steering committee actually needs to sign off.
Present the full technical architecture diagram in complete implementation detail, so the committee understands exactly how each subagent operates and validates its output internally.
Skip a high-level description and move straight into an implementation demo, since watching the system work explains it better than words would.
Describe input → processing → output → feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against case-outcome and cost goals, without implementation detail.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of case-outcome and cost evaluation, not implementation internals. A is insufficient detail; B is too much of the wrong kind of detail; C skips the communication need entirely.

questions.prompt: A competing vendor proposes a single, generalist agent with all tools (document processing, privilege detection, redaction, production formatting) rather than a coordinator with specialized subagents.

choices.text: A single generalist agent scales better as tool count grows, since one unified schema can register unlimited tools without added complexity.
Specialized subagents are strictly a cost-increasing choice, since splitting work across multiple calls only adds overhead with no reliability upside at all.
There's no meaningful architectural difference between a single generalist agent and a coordinator with specialized subagents at this particular tool count.
A single agent holding every tool and responsibility is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than specialized subagents scoped narrowly.

questions.explanation: A single generalist agent holding every tool and responsibility is more exposed to degraded tool-selection reliability than agents scoped to narrower roles — the core argument for specialization. A, B, and C understate or deny this real architectural tradeoff.
