questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only fraud-catch rate and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Treat fraud-catch rate alone as sufficient, since it's the system's stated primary purpose.
Define metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety as first-class targets.
Treat latency and cost as operations concerns with no bearing on evaluation design.
Treat safety metrics as relevant only to more heavily regulated industries than payments.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it catches fraud. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past transactions.

choices.text: Treat a single automated method against a fixed labeled set as sufficient for any production system.
Replace the automated checks entirely with human review of every flagged transaction.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely, treating dataset size as the sole improvement lever.
Use mixed methods: automated eval for scale, human review for nuance, adversarial testing for safety paths.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and C each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new prompt version improves triage precision before rolling it out to all traffic.

choices.text: Roll the new prompt out to all traffic immediately and monitor informally for problems.
Change the prompt and the model tier at the same time, to maximize potential improvement.
Skip testing, on the assumption prompt changes are inherently low-risk.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; C dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: A flagged transaction was wrongly cleared as legitimate. Investigation shows the underlying risk-signal data was correct and retrieved properly, and the model's response paraphrased it inaccurately.

choices.text: Treat this as a generation issue and fix the prompt or add output validation to catch inaccurate paraphrasing.
Treat this as a retrieval problem and rework the indexing pipeline.
Conclude this can't be diagnosed without retraining the underlying model.
Treat this as a model-tier mismatch requiring an upgrade to the next capability tier, regardless of what the investigation actually showed.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. B and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; C avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled risk-signal feed refresh, the system starts flagging legitimate transactions as fraud, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model provider silently pushed an update to the underlying model.
Suspect a temperature setting changed, assuming that would make flagging behavior perfectly deterministic again.
Suspect the context window shrank, cutting off part of the risk signal.
Investigate the retrieval/ingestion layer first, since the regression tracks the feed refresh.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/ingestion. A, B, and C would not specifically correlate with a feed refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency but is worried about hurting fraud-catch accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Optimize cost, latency, and accuracy independently, treating each as unrelated to the others.
Maximize accuracy regardless of cost or latency, since fraud-catch is the system's core job.
Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget.
Treat this tradeoff as unmeasurable, something that can only be guessed at.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and B optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average precision score.

choices.text: Treat a single aggregate weekly average as sufficient for production monitoring.
Track only cost in monitoring, since the eval suite alone already covers accuracy.
Surface drift via per-merchant-category or per-transaction-type breakdowns, not just an aggregate.
Treat weekly granularity as always sufficient, regardless of how the system is behaving.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. A and D accept a monitoring blind spot; B drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting manual review of flagged transactions by 80%, citing a 97% aggregate precision score.

choices.text: Proceed with the 80% review cut based on the 97% aggregate figure alone.
Treat aggregate accuracy as definitionally representative of every merchant segment.
Segment accuracy by merchant category and transaction type before cutting review.
Refuse any reduction in human review, regardless of what the measured accuracy shows.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by merchant category and transaction type before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. A and B trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prompt version improves fraud-catch rate but the team hasn't checked whether it also increased the false-positive rate on legitimate high-value transactions.

choices.text: Check the false-positive rate on high-value legitimate transactions before shipping the change.
Treat fraud-catch rate alone as a sufficient signal to ship the new prompt version.
Treat false-positive behavior as something evaluation is structurally unable to measure, unlike fraud-catch rate itself.
Ship the change and monitor informally afterward instead of testing it beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated fraud-catch improvement could mask a worsened false-positive rate on legitimate transactions; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. B and D ship without adequate testing; C incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of correctly-flagged fraud alerts are rated as low quality by the fraud-ops team, who cite unclear reasoning in the alert write-up.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric's validation logic itself is broken and discard the metric entirely.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always raises ops satisfaction.
Investigate explanation clarity or actionability as a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.
Ignore fraud-ops satisfaction scores and rely on the accuracy metric alone.

questions.explanation: "Correct but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (explanation clarity, actionability) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; B assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends full transaction history plus a large static risk-policy document on every turn of multi-turn triage-review conversations.

choices.text: Treat this as unoptimizable, since full transaction history is always required on every turn.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever considered for reducing token cost.
Cache the static risk-policy document and trim or summarize older review-conversation turns.
Remove the risk-policy document entirely from the prompt to save tokens.

questions.explanation: Caching the static risk-policy document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn review conversations. A denies an obvious lever; D removes needed content; B is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production system, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Treat raw logging at full volume, already structured by timestamp and request ID, as sufficient observability on its own.
Reduce logging volume to save storage cost, with no other change to the approach.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged categories, segment metrics.
Treat observability as needing no structure as long as the data is retained somewhere.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable, however consistently they're timestamped. A and D accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a specific quality regression was caused by a recent prompt change, a recent model version change, or a risk-data change — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: Assume the most recently shipped change is always the cause of a regression.
Treat attribution as impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week.
Revert all three changes without investigating which one, if any, actually caused the regression, to be safe.
Isolate and re-test each of the three changes independently to attribute the regression correctly.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and C guess without evidence; B gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a fraud-explanation output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: Conclude the model is malfunctioning and needs retraining.
Loosen the schema slightly and make the reference string longer, on the theory that either change fixes the failures.
Replace exact-string-match with a check for required content/structure, since output isn't fully deterministic.
Increase the temperature setting to fix the intermittent eval failures.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; B doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Cascade Pay triages flagged transactions to decide which get auto-cleared, auto-blocked, or escalated to a human fraud analyst. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the fraud-triage system is, to track over time.

choices.text: Treat a single number as always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs.
Use a top-line number, but pair it with segment-level and multi-dimensional detail underneath.
Use fraud-catch rate alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric to leadership, under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and C oversimplify to a single lossy number; D refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data flow, retention, and access-logging design in the final week before launch, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: Treat this sequencing as low-risk, since compliance requirements can always be layered on right before launch with minor patches.
Recognize that GDPR-driven requirements can force costly structural retrofits this late in a build.
Treat compliance as affecting only legal documentation, not system architecture.
Treat HIPAA, not GDPR, as the relevant regime for a European retail bank.

questions.explanation: GDPR-driven requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and C understate real architectural impact; D misidentifies the applicable regulatory regime.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single output the customer-service system produces, framing it as the safest governance posture.

choices.text: Target human-in-the-loop at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions, not every output.
Require maximal human review on every output, as the correct default for banking AI systems.
Treat human reviewers as categorically less accurate than the model across every decision type, making review counterproductive.
Treat blanket review on every output as required by GDPR, regardless of other considerations.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. B and C overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; D misattributes this requirement to GDPR, which doesn't mandate it.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from customer-submitted free text, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: Address these risks only once they're actually observed happening in production.
Design a mitigation for each failure mode up front — grounding, input isolation, consistency checks.
Treat these risks as exclusive to non-banking use cases.
Rely on a single generic guardrail to address hallucination, injection, and inconsistency equally well.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, consistency checks for output drift) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; D assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; C is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: Stakeholders ask whether the system's lending-related outputs could produce disparate outcomes across different customer demographics.

choices.text: Treat this as a legal/compliance matter entirely, with no architectural concern before launch.
Evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population and measure for disparate impact.
Treat disparate impact as impossible in an LLM-based system by construction.
Treat this concern as relevant only to systems making the final lending decision outright.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. A defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The 40-person compliance-operations team's Claude Code usage is inconsistent — some staff have team conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by machine.

choices.text: Have each of the 40 staff individually troubleshoot their own local configuration.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer to reduce variance across the team.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of rolling AI tooling out to a large team.
Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team level.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. A and C leave the systemic cause unaddressed; B sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The team wants Claude Code-generated code changes in this banking context to go through the same review rigor as any other change to a regulated system.

choices.text: Let AI-assisted code bypass the standard review process entirely, since it was "written by AI" rather than by a human engineer.
Apply only a spot-check to AI-generated code, rather than the standard review process.
Apply a lower review bar to AI-generated code than to human-written code in this system.
Keep standard SDLC review, testing, and version-control practices unchanged, regardless of who generated the diff.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a regulated system. A, B, and C all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: A production incident traces back to a Claude Code-generated data-handling change. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated code logic or in how the surrounding system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug is in the generated code without investigating the integration layer at all.
Disable Claude Code for the team entirely, since generated code can never be adequately validated.
Triage it like any incident: use traces/logs to localize whether the failure is in integration or in the generated logic.
Roll back every recent Claude Code-assisted change across the whole platform, regardless of whether it's related to this specific incident.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and D skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance-operations team wants a documented, repeatable workflow for a recurring task (generating a weekly GDPR data-subject-request summary report) versus a one-off exploratory coding task.

choices.text: Build both the recurring report and the one-off task as ad hoc, undocumented prompts each time.
Package the recurring report as a Skill for reuse; leave the one-off task as an ad hoc session.
Build both the recurring report and the one-off exploratory task as dedicated MCP servers.
Build the recurring workflow and the one-off task using identical tooling and structure.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; C over-engineers the one-off task; D ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance team wants documented evidence of who accessed what customer data through the system and when, to satisfy GDPR accountability obligations.

choices.text: Design access control and audit logging as explicit architectural components, not an implicit byproduct.
Treat access logging as optional, as long as the system already has role-based permissions and single sign-on configured.
Treat audit logging as something that can be added later without any architectural impact.
Log only failed access attempts, since those are the ones accountability reviews typically ask about.

questions.explanation: Access control and audit logging need to be explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an incidental byproduct, especially under GDPR accountability obligations. B, C, and D each understate what compliance-grade audit evidence actually requires.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The steering committee for this deployment includes retail-banking, legal/compliance, and engineering stakeholders with different priorities and vocabularies.

choices.text: Tailor communication to each audience — tradeoffs framed in terms retail-banking and legal can evaluate.
Communicate only with engineering stakeholders, trusting them to relay information to the others.
Skip stakeholder communication with retail-banking and legal until the system is fully built.
Use identical technical documentation for all three audiences, to save preparation effort.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by retail-banking, legal, and engineering audiences alike. B, C, and D each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: Midway through the project, the compliance team's requirements shift meaningfully based on new EDPB regulatory guidance.

choices.text: Refuse to incorporate the EDPB-driven change, since requirements were already agreed upon.
Incorporate the change silently, without informing stakeholders of its downstream impact.
Restart the entire project from scratch, regardless of how narrow the change's actual scope is.
Re-engage discovery for the affected scope and communicate the tradeoff to stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally-driven requirements shift. A and B mishandle a real change; C disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: After launch, the architect's involvement is discussed as ending at handoff to Alderbrook's operations team.

choices.text: Extend lifecycle responsibility through monitoring and iteration, treating production signal as an architectural hook back into the design rather than stopping at handoff.
Treat lifecycle responsibility as ending once the contract with Alderbrook is signed.
Treat monitoring as necessary only if a major incident eventually occurs.
Treat handoff as correct: monitoring and iteration become entirely the operations team's responsibility.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle management extends through monitoring and iteration based on production signal, not just through handoff. B, C, and D all end architectural responsibility earlier than the lifecycle model calls for.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: Documentation for this system currently lists final configuration values (model tier, retry settings, thresholds) with no explanation of why each was chosen.

choices.text: Treat listing final configuration values as sufficient, since the "what" is all a future team needs.
Treat documenting reasoning as unnecessary overhead, especially in a regulated environment.
Restrict modification rights to the original architect, making further documentation moot.
Capture the "why" behind key decisions — compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning — alongside the "what."

questions.explanation: Capturing the "why" (compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning) alongside the "what" is what lets a future team safely extend the system, especially in a regulated context. A, B, and C all leave that reasoning undocumented and effectively lost.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance-operations team wants Claude Code to help with routine tasks (drafting documentation, exploring an unfamiliar module) but is unsure where it actually saves meaningful time versus adding review overhead.

choices.text: Assume AI-assisted tooling saves time on every task category by default, without measuring it.
Ban Claude Code for all documentation tasks without evaluating where it actually helps.
Mandate Claude Code usage for all tasks, regardless of measured benefit.
Evaluate specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead.

questions.explanation: Evaluating specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead gives an evidence-based answer instead of assuming a blanket benefit either way. A and C over-assume benefit; B forecloses potential benefit without evaluation.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Alderbrook Bank, a European retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that processes customer service requests containing personal data and assists a 40-person compliance-operations team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: A recurring operational issue is that different engineers debug similar Claude Code integration failures independently, each re-deriving the same integration-layer-versus-model-output triage process.

choices.text: Accept the redundant re-derivation across the team as an ongoing inefficiency with no realistic architectural fix available.
Document the triage process for distinguishing integration-layer failures from model-output failures.
Restrict debugging on this system to a single designated engineer.
Conclude the issue can only be resolved by switching to a different tool entirely.

questions.explanation: Documenting the shared triage process turns individually re-derived knowledge into reusable operational knowledge, directly addressing the redundant-effort problem described. A accepts avoidable inefficiency; C and D propose disproportionate structural changes instead of the straightforward documentation fix. --- *End of Practice Exam 5.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the client's real goal is to reduce dwell time at distribution hubs by 30% using existing staff and equipment — not new capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around efficiency, building success metrics around dwell-time reduction per existing resource rather than novel capability.
Frame the architecture around transformation, arguing dwell-time reduction is best achieved by introducing new automation capability the current process lacks entirely.
Frame the architecture around cost reduction, since dwell-time savings ultimately translate into lower labor and equipment spend across the network.
Skip framing around a specific value pillar, since the system's technical success will speak for itself once deployed across every hub.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (dwell-time reduction with existing staff/equipment) is an efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both the architecture and its success metrics. B chases a transformation narrative discovery didn't support; C misnames the pillar; D skips framing that keeps the project aligned to what discovery actually found.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The customs-documentation validation step follows the same fixed sequence of checks for every shipment type, regardless of contents or destination, with no branching based on intermediate findings.

choices.text: Treat it as an agentic pattern, since orchestration steps always benefit from letting the model decide its own branching autonomously.
Treat it as a single augmented LLM call, since a document check with no branching is inherently too simple to model as steps.
Treat it as a fixed workflow, since the steps are identical and predetermined for every shipment type regardless of contents or destination.
Choose whichever pattern requires the least tooling investment to stand up, since the three patterns are functionally interchangeable for a routine compliance check like this one.

questions.explanation: Steps that are identical and predetermined regardless of case specifics are the defining case for a fixed workflow. A overstates the autonomy needed; B undersells the sequencing actually required; D ignores that the patterns have real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to four specialized subagents (procurement, carrier selection, routing optimization, exception handling).

choices.text: Let subagents communicate directly with whichever subagent needs the result next, minimizing hops and removing the coordinator from routine handoffs.
Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability and consistent error handling across the pipeline.
Merge all four responsibilities into a single subagent, avoiding coordination overhead entirely by collapsing procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling into one component.
Let subagents communicate directly, but log the traffic afterward for review, treating logging as an equivalent substitute for coordinator-mediated routing.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. A and D sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; C discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents in the first place.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Every subagent completes its assigned work correctly, but the coordinator's decomposition only routes domestic shipments to the pipeline — international shipments requiring customs handling are never routed to any subagent and silently fall through.

choices.text: Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers every shipment category, including international shipments, rather than tuning subagents.
Add a prompt instruction telling each subagent to flag any shipment type it doesn't recognize, without changing how shipments get routed.
Give the existing subagents broader tool access so any subagent could in principle handle any shipment type that reaches it.
Add a fifth subagent specifically scoped to edge-case shipments, leaving the coordinator's existing routing logic and category coverage completely unchanged going forward.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while whole shipment categories are never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. B, C, and D all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The design must align technical architecture to a specific business value pillar Meridian actually cares about, distinct from a generic "we added AI" narrative.

choices.text: Business value pillars are fundamentally a sales and marketing concern, not something that should constrain technical architecture or system design.
Efficiency, resilience, cost, and service-level are examples of such pillars; the one actually chosen should drive both architecture and success metrics.
Any AI system inherently demonstrates transformation just by being built, so no additional framing around a specific pillar is required.
The pillar should be selected after the system ships, based on whichever benefit turns out to be easiest to measure retroactively.

questions.explanation: Business value pillars (efficiency, resilience, cost, service-level) give both the architecture and its metrics a clear anchor. A, C, and D all skip or defer this framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Meridian's dispatch team is skeptical of automated routing decisions and worried about accountability if a shipment is misrouted; discovery interviews surface this repeatedly.

choices.text: Recommend against the project entirely, since dispatcher skepticism about accountability for a misrouted shipment signals the organization isn't ready for automated routing decisions at all.
Proceed with the technical design unchanged and let change management handle the skepticism separately, with no input into the architecture.
Ignore the sentiment, since accountability worries aren't a structured technical requirement and therefore fall outside the scope of the architecture.
Treat it as a real implicit constraint alongside explicit requirements — it should shape rollout sequencing and checkpoints.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment is a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter — it's discovery input, not noise to ignore. A and C treat it as out of scope; B overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing it against the technical case.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why the exception-handling subagent (weather, customs, disruptions) uses a higher-capability, higher-cost model tier than the load-consolidation subagent.

choices.text: Explain the tradeoff explicitly: exception handling needs deeper reasoning over ambiguous, high-stakes situations, which justifies the added cost and latency versus load consolidation.
Use the same model tier everywhere for simplicity, regardless of how much reasoning depth each subagent's specific task actually requires.
Tell the stakeholder that the higher tier is used simply because exception handling is more organizationally important, without elaborating on the underlying reasoning or tradeoffs involved.
Avoid explaining the tier differences at all, since stakeholders generally don't need or want this level of technical detail.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. C and D withhold the reasoning stakeholders need; B removes a deliberate, justified difference for false simplicity.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Networks operates a multi-modal freight network spanning ocean, rail, and truck carriers. It wants to modernize procurement, carrier selection, routing, and exception handling (customs delays, weather disruptions, capacity shortfalls) with a Claude-powered orchestration platform. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The architecture's current design produces a final routing recommendation with no mechanism to learn from dispatcher overrides or actual delivery outcomes over time.

choices.text: Add a feedback loop capturing dispatcher overrides and delivery outcomes as a first-class architectural component, so the system can improve after deployment.
Treat this as acceptable, since the initial design already reflects current best practice and further iteration isn't architecturally necessary.
Treat feedback loops as a data science concern unrelated to the architecture, since they involve model retraining rather than system design.
Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase, with no data-capture hooks in the current design to support adding one later without significant rework.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures dispatcher overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve after deployment. B, C, and D all treat a first-class architectural component as optional or someone else's problem.

questions.prompt: The client wants a single enhanced LLM call — with lookup of carrier contract terms — to answer straightforward rate-lookup questions from dispatchers, without any multi-step autonomous orchestration.

choices.text: This calls for a full multi-agent architecture that independently validates each carrier-contract lookup, regardless of how simple the dispatcher's rate-lookup task actually is.
This requires a fixed workflow with at least five sequential validation steps, even though the dispatcher's request is a single lookup question.
This cannot be built with Claude at all, since answering a rate question without an autonomous agent isn't technically possible.
An augmented LLM pattern — a single call enhanced with carrier-contract retrieval and tools — fits this simpler augmentation need without the overhead of multi-step agentic orchestration.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with retrieval, without multi-step autonomous orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern is for. A and B over-engineer a simple augmentation need; C is factually wrong.

choices.text: This capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability; the unrelated notification and invoicing tools should be removed or moved to a better-suited subagent.
This has no architectural downside as long as the procurement subagent's system prompt clearly and thoroughly explains when to use each additional unrelated tool.
More tools always improve a subagent's flexibility, so adding customer notifications and invoicing should be encouraged rather than questioned.
The fix is to increase the subagent's context window so it can hold instructions for all of its tools more comfortably.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows — the fix is removing or relocating them, not writing around it with more prompt text. B and C ignore this real degradation; D doesn't address selection reliability at all.

choices.text: Run carrier selection and exception-check as independent, parallel subagent calls once procurement completes, instead of processing them sequentially.
Sequential processing is required for auditability, since a parallel execution trace would be significantly harder for reviewers to reconstruct after the fact.
Parallelization isn't possible within a coordinator/subagent architecture, since subagents can only be invoked one at a time by design.
Combine carrier selection and exception-check into a single subagent, sidestepping the sequencing question rather than exploiting the independence between them.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (procurement) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. B and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

A single agent holding every tool and responsibility is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than specialized subagents scoped narrowly.

Document the architecture and the reasoning behind key decisions — pattern choices, decomposition boundaries, tier selections — not just the final configuration values a future team would otherwise have to re-derive.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most attorney queries are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many precedents, and a small fraction are simple citation lookups.

choices.text: Always use the fastest tier to minimize cost, accepting quality loss on complex questions since most queries are only moderately complex anyway.
Always use the highest-capability tier to guarantee quality on every question, treating the added cost and latency difference as immaterial given the platform's query volume.
Route based on task difficulty — a fast, low-temperature tier for simple lookups, a balanced tier for typical questions, and a high-capability tier for deep multi-step cases.
Use one fixed, structured model tier for every question regardless of complexity, since a single tier is simpler to operate and monitor.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. A and B ignore fit-to-task; D sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (legal-analyst persona, citation format, formatting rules) followed by retrieved case excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Order doesn't affect cost or latency for this use case, since the API processes the entire prompt as a single unit regardless of arrangement.
Put the retrieved case excerpts first, since they're most relevant to the specific query the attorney actually asked.
Alternate system-prompt instructions and retrieved case content throughout the prompt so relevant material always stays close to the instructions it's meant to support.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable caching, with retrieved excerpts after it, cutting latency and cost.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, B, and C all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Lex Meridian's corpus mixes long-form case opinions and briefs with short structured records (statute citation tables with section numbers and effective dates).

choices.text: Chunking and indexing strategy should match each data shape — long-form opinions need different treatment than short structured statute records, or retrieval quality degrades for whichever type doesn't match.
One chunking and indexing strategy tuned for long-form documents can serve both content types equally well without any adjustment.
Structured statute records should be excluded from retrieval entirely, since the corpus's indexing was designed around long-form opinions.
Use the largest possible chunk size for everything, avoiding the need to maintain multiple chunking schemas across content types.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. B and D ignore this mismatch; C discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorney queries range from exact lookups ("what is the statute of limitations under Section 12.4") to conceptual questions ("how has the doctrine of promissory estoppel evolved across circuits").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type, including exact statutory lookups where a section number is already known and easily validated.

Query pattern doesn't meaningfully affect which retrieval approach is appropriate here, since embeddings alone can resolve both exact statutory lookups and open-ended conceptual questions equally well.
Use only structured or metadata filtering for every query type, including open-ended conceptual questions about how a doctrine has evolved.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern: structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and C force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; B denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorneys need citations that reliably map each legal claim to a specific case, page, and pin cite, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Require structured output pairing each claim with its source — case name, citation, excerpt — so citation mapping survives synthesis instead of being reconstructed from memory.
Ask the model, in prose, to always cite its sources thoroughly, trusting that instruction alone to preserve accurate claim-to-case mapping.
Add citations after the fact by searching for a plausible case that could support each claim once the response is drafted.
Append a general bibliography of every case consulted at the end of each response, without tying specific claims to specific sources.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. B, C, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Two retrieved cases disagree on whether a particular circuit still follows a specific precedent — one appears to have been implicitly overruled by a later, uncited opinion.

choices.text: Average or blend the two conflicting positions into a single stated rule, presenting it as the circuit's settled current law.
Present both positions explicitly, flagged as a discrepancy, with citations, rather than silently picking one.
Always prefer whichever case was retrieved first, treating retrieval order as a reasonable, defensible tiebreaker between two conflicting appellate authorities.
Omit the point of law entirely from the response, since the two retrieved sources disagree on the applicable rule.

questions.explanation: Presenting both positions with citations, flagged as a discrepancy, preserves the actual information for the attorney rather than resolving a real discrepancy arbitrarily. A, C, and D all discard or obscure a genuine legal conflict.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with citation fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Repeat the system prompt instruction more emphatically, restating the JSON validity requirement several times to make it harder for the model to ignore.
Use tool-use or schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose alone.
Post-process every response to strip any leading text that appears before the first opening brace of the JSON payload.
Increase max_tokens to leave enough room for both the conversational preamble and the full structured JSON that follows it.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; D doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform needs to connect to a proprietary internal brief-bank system, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond just this research platform.

choices.text: Build an MCP server exposing the brief-bank operations as tools and resources, reusable across internal Claude-powered tools.
Hard-code the brief-bank integration directly into this research platform's own application code, since it's the primary and most frequent consumer of that data today.
Paste the entire brief-bank corpus into every prompt so each internal tool has full access without needing a shared integration layer.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own brief-bank integration independently, since requirements may differ slightly between tools.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. B, C, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding between exposing the full case-law catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Loading the full case-law catalog up front is always preferable for completeness, since the agent then never needs to issue a follow-up query.
There's no meaningful difference in context cost between loading the full catalog and querying it on demand as the corpus grows.
The catalog should never be exposed to the agent in any form, since catalog access introduces an unnecessary retrieval dependency.
Progressive discovery — querying a catalog resource as needed — scales better than loading the entire catalog into context up front, especially as the corpus grows.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. A and B ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; C removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: An attorney asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several retrieved opinions before concluding on a multi-jurisdictional issue.

choices.text: A chain-of-thought approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, suits this kind of multi-document synthesis question.
Zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance is always equally effective, regardless of how many documents or jurisdictions the question spans.
Chain-of-thought prompting is only useful for coding and mathematical tasks, since legal synthesis across jurisdictions doesn't benefit from explicit intermediate reasoning steps or scratch work.
The model cannot reason across multiple retrieved documents at all, regardless of which prompting approach is used to guide it.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning. B, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, disclaimer language, formatting rules) across several different attorney-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Use modular, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — a maintainability lever distinct from caching or Skills.
Duplicate the citation-format and disclaimer fragments into each feature's prompt independently, updating every copy whenever the language changes.
Modular prompts are the same underlying mechanism as prompt caching, so enabling caching accomplishes the standardization the team wants.

Standardization of shared citation and disclaimer language across features isn't realistically achievable through prompt design alone, and instead requires building a separate configuration microservice to own it.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. B reintroduces duplication; C conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate the holding of a correctly retrieved case.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as sufficient evidence of correctness, since a confident, properly cited response with clean formatting is unlikely to misstate a case's holding.
This is not something an architecture can address; it's purely a model limitation with no available mitigation at the system level.
Apply defensive validation — verify the stated holding against the source excerpt rather than trusting confident phrasing.
Increase output length so there's more room within the response for the holding to be stated correctly and in full.

questions.explanation: Verifying the stated holding against the source excerpt catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; D doesn't address correctness; B incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether attorney-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection for the research platform.

choices.text: Latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions, since accuracy is the only dimension attorneys actually care about.
Yes — model tier selection should weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the use case's SLA can tolerate, not default to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
Only cost should factor into tier selection, never latency, since attorneys can simply wait longer for a more accurate answer.
SLAs are purely a stakeholder-communication concern with no bearing on technical architecture or model tier selection decisions.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, C, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. It wants Claude to answer research questions using both general legal reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of opinions, statutes, and briefs. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Upgrade immediately without testing, since improved benchmark scores guarantee the new version will perform at least as well in production.
Pin the current version in production, increase test coverage, and evaluate the new release against the platform's own tests before upgrading, since behavior can shift.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen, since any version change risks destabilizing the production system.
Continue floating to latest automatically in production, since a newer model version with better published benchmark numbers is always an improvement for a legal research use case.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; C over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Lex Meridian is a legal research platform used by attorneys to research case law, statutes, and internal firm briefs. choices.text: Input and output token budgets are entirely independent of each other, so retrieved-content volume never constrains the length of an answer.
Output length has no practical limit regardless of how much retrieved content occupies the input, so budgeting isn't necessary.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so architects must balance retrieved-content volume against the room needed for a detailed, well-cited answer.
This tradeoff only matters for unusually long documents, never for the typical attorney query the platform handles day to day.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and D all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.
