questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only forecast-adoption rate (how often reps accept the copilot's suggested numbers) and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Latency and cost are operations concerns unrelated to evaluation design, since evaluation should focus purely on whether reps find the forecast accurate enough to adopt in practice.
Safety metrics are only relevant for regulated industries, so a sales-forecasting copilot doesn't need them as first-class evaluation criteria.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security as first-class metrics — an adopted but slow, expensive, or unsafe system still fails overall.
Adoption rate alone is sufficient, since it's the system's stated purpose and already captures whether reps find the forecasts useful.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it gets adopted. A, B, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past forecasts.

choices.text: A single automated, structured check is sufficient for any production system, since automated checks scale better than any manual review process.
Replace the automated accuracy checks entirely with human review, since only a person can judge whether a forecast explanation is nuanced enough.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely as the sole improvement lever, adding more historical forecasts until automated accuracy plateaus.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for safety-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and C each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new prompt version improves forecast-accuracy explanations before rolling it out to all sales regions.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all regions immediately and monitor for problems, since a staged rollout would only delay the improvement reps are waiting for.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any observed difference can be attributed to that one change.
Change the prompt and the model tier simultaneously to maximize the potential improvement observed in the explanation quality.
Skip testing entirely, since prompt changes to an explanation feature are inherently low-risk and don't warrant a controlled comparison.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips a controlled comparison; C confounds two variables; D dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: A forecast explanation is factually wrong about a deal's stage. Investigation shows the underlying CRM data was correct and retrieved properly, and the model's response paraphrased it inaccurately.

choices.text: This is a retrieval problem, so the fix belongs in the indexing pipeline even though the CRM data itself was validated and retrieved correctly.
This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue, calling for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.
This cannot be diagnosed at all without retraining the underlying model on a larger set of deal-stage examples.
This is a model mismatch requiring a different, higher-capability model tier across the board, regardless of what the specific failure-mode investigation actually turned up in this case.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. A and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; C avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled CRM data sync, the copilot starts producing confident but incorrect pipeline-stage summaries, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider, since a behavior change without a corresponding architecture change points at the model.
Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression tracks the data-sync event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since deterministic, non-random output shouldn't otherwise start looking confident but wrong immediately after a routine, unrelated data sync.
Suspect the context window shrank, since a smaller window would explain confident but incorrect pipeline-stage summaries appearing suddenly.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data-sync event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, C, and D would not specifically correlate with a CRM data sync.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency but is worried about hurting forecast accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, in isolation, since tuning them together makes the tradeoffs harder to reason about.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of cost or latency implications, since a wrong forecast is worse than a slow one.
This tradeoff cannot be measured, only guessed at, since cost, latency, and accuracy interact in ways too complex to quantify.

Optimize cost, latency, and accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest, fastest configuration that fails the accuracy bar isn't a win, and neither is maximizing accuracy at unsustainable cost.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. A and B optimize dimensions in isolation; C claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall monthly average forecast-accuracy score across all sales regions.

choices.text: A single aggregate average is sufficient for production monitoring, since regional and deal-type variation should statistically wash out at a large enough sample size.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is already captured by the eval suite run separately from production monitoring.
Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-region or per-deal-type breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a specific failing segment.
Monthly granularity is always sufficient regardless of how the system's behavior actually changes week to week across regions.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate monthly average can hide. A and D accept a monitoring blind spot; B drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting human review of flagged low-confidence forecasts by 80%, citing a 95% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Proceed with the cut based on the 95% aggregate figure alone, since that number already reflects performance across every region and deal type the system serves.
Aggregate accuracy is definitionally representative of every segment, so no further breakdown is needed before changing the review process.
Human review should never be reduced regardless of measured accuracy, since any cut to review coverage is inherently too risky.
Segment accuracy by region and deal type before cutting review, since the aggregate figure can mask a specific segment performing far worse than the average.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by region and deal type before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. A and B trust the aggregate uncritically; C over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prompt version improves forecast-adoption rate, but the team has not checked whether it also changed the rate of overconfident forecasts on genuinely volatile, hard-to-predict deals.

choices.text: Adoption rate alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change, since reps accepting more forecasts implies the explanations are better.

Overconfidence on volatile, genuinely hard-to-predict deals is not something the current evaluation setup can reliably measure, so it isn't reasonable to expect the team to check for it before shipping.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact, instead of testing for the overconfidence failure mode before rollout.
Check the overconfidence failure mode specifically before shipping — an adoption-rate gain could mask worse overconfidence on hard deals.

questions.explanation: An isolated adoption-rate improvement could mask a worsened overconfidence failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and C ship without adequate testing; B incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of forecasts are technically accurate but rated poorly by sales managers in feedback surveys.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric itself is broken and discard it, since a technically accurate forecast shouldn't ever be rated poorly by a manager.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves manager satisfaction regardless of what's actually driving the low ratings.

Investigate a dimension beyond factual accuracy — e.g., clarity, actionability, or explanation quality — since "accurate but poorly rated" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.
Ignore manager satisfaction scores in favor of the accuracy metric alone, since accuracy is the harder, more objective thing to measure.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (clarity, actionability, explanation quality) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; B assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends full deal history plus a large static forecasting-methodology document on every turn of multi-turn coaching conversations.

choices.text: This has no optimization opportunity, since full deal history and the methodology document are always required on every single turn.
Remove the static methodology document entirely to save tokens, since coaching conversations rarely reference it directly by name.
Apply prompt caching to the static methodology document and trim or summarize older turns of deal history to reduce redundant token cost.
Switch to a smaller, more structured model as the only lever for reducing token cost, since caching the static content wouldn't meaningfully help here.

questions.explanation: Caching the static methodology document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. A denies an obvious lever; B removes needed content; D is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production copilot, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy, since every request and every response is technically captured somewhere for a reviewer to search later if needed.
Reduce logging to save storage cost, with no other change to how failure patterns get identified from what remains.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged categories, segment metrics — since raw logs alone aren't reviewable.
Observability requires no particular structure as long as the raw data is retained somewhere the team could theoretically search later.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and D accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a specific quality regression was caused by a recent prompt change, a recent model version change, or a CRM schema change — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: This is why changes should be rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each one.
Assume the most recent change is always the cause, since it's the last thing that shipped before the regression appeared.

Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week, so the team should stop trying to isolate a single cause and instead treat the regression as an unresolved, permanent mystery.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which one, if any, actually caused the observed regression.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. B and D guess without evidence; C gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a forecast-explanation output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: The model is malfunctioning and needs retraining, since a valid explanation should always exactly match the fixed reference string.
The reference string needs to be longer, so there's a better chance the model's deterministic phrasing happens to pass validation and align with it.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content or structure instead of exact text.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures, since more randomness should eventually produce a string that happens to match exactly.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. A and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; B doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and A/B Testing of a Sales-Forecasting Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Northwind Sales Intelligence built a Claude-powered copilot that helps sales reps and managers produce and explain pipeline forecasts. It's been in production for four months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and running controlled tests of proposed changes.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the sales-forecasting copilot is, to track over time.

choices.text: A single number is always achievable and sufficient for any system's evaluation needs, regardless of how many dimensions actually matter.
Use forecast-adoption rate alone as the single number, since it's the system's stated purpose and the easiest metric to report.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric under any circumstances, since leadership shouldn't be given an oversimplified view.

A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be presented alongside segment-level and multi-dimensional detail — accuracy, latency, cost, safety — so it doesn't mask a failing area.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and B oversimplify to a single lossy number; C refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data residency, retention, and access-logging design in the final weeks before a multi-country rollout, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: This sequencing carries no risk, since compliance requirements like residency and retention can always be added right before a launch.
Cross-border data-residency, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.
Compliance only affects legal documentation, not system architecture, so it can be finalized independently of how the application was built.
A single global data-residency policy is sufficient regardless of which countries are actually involved in the multi-country rollout, since the underlying platform is identical everywhere.

questions.explanation: Cross-border data-residency, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and C understate real architectural impact; D wrongly assumes a single policy suffices across jurisdictions.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single quality-flag output the production-line system produces, framing it as the safest governance posture.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every single quality-flag output is always the correct default posture for a manufacturing safety system, regardless of the actual error cost or ambiguity involved in a given case.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost decisions instead.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model at this task, making review of any kind counterproductive.
This blanket-review approach is required by ISO certification, regardless of what the actual error costs or workload considerations are.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and C overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; D misattributes this to a certification regime not established by the scenario.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from operator-submitted free-text notes, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: Design mitigations for each known failure mode up front — grounding for hallucination, input isolation for injection, output validation for consistency — rather than reactively.
These risks only need to be addressed if they're actually observed in production first, since preemptive mitigation wastes design effort.
A single generic guardrail addresses hallucination, injection, and inconsistency equally well, since all three ultimately stem from the same root cause.
These risks are exclusive to non-manufacturing use cases, since a quality-flagging system operating on a production line never actually processes operator-submitted free text notes.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. B defers to a reactive posture; C assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; D is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: Plant management asks whether the quality-flagging system's decisions could produce disparate outcomes across different production lines or shifts with different staffing demographics.

choices.text: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population of lines and shifts and measure for disparate impact rather than assuming it's absent.
This is not an architectural concern at all; it belongs entirely to legal and compliance review after the system has already launched.
Disparate impact is impossible in an LLM-based quality-flagging system by construction, since the model has no access to staffing demographics.
This concern only applies to systems making final personnel decisions directly, not to any assistive quality-flagging system like this one.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. B defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The 40-person plant-engineering team's Claude Code usage is inconsistent across country sites — some engineers have team conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by machine.

choices.text: Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer across every site, reducing variance by eliminating most of the team's actual day-to-day usage of the tool entirely.
Have each engineer individually troubleshoot their own local configuration and MCP server access as issues come up at their site.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable cost of rolling out AI tooling across multiple countries and plant sites.
Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team level so behavior doesn't depend on local setup.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. B and C leave the systemic cause unaddressed; A sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The team wants Claude Code-generated code changes to production-line control tooling to go through the same review rigor as any other change to a safety-relevant system.

choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review entirely, since a change drafted by Claude Code was effectively already checked during the generation and drafting process itself.
Only a spot-check of AI-generated code is necessary, since the generation process already screens out most likely defects.
Review requirements should be lower for AI-generated code than for human-written code, given how the change was originally produced.
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the rigor a safety-relevant system requires.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a safety-relevant system. A, B, and C all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for this context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: A production incident traces back to a Claude Code-generated change to a data-logging module at one plant. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated code logic or in how the surrounding system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug is in the generated code without further investigation or validation, since that's the component that changed most recently.
Disable Claude Code for the entire team following any incident, regardless of where the actual fault is eventually traced to.
Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the code/model output — using traces and logs to localize the actual failure point.
Roll back every recent Claude Code-assisted change across every plant, regardless of whether it's related to the logging module.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and D skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The plant-engineering team wants a documented, repeatable workflow for a recurring task (generating a weekly cross-plant quality-metrics rollup) versus a one-off exploratory debugging task at a single site.

choices.text: Build both the recurring rollup and the one-off debugging task as ad hoc, undocumented prompts each time either one comes up.

Build both the recurring cross-plant rollup and the one-off single-site debugging task as standing MCP servers regardless of reuse profile, since infrastructure investment is worth it for any workflow, recurring or not.
Package the recurring, well-defined rollup workflow as a Skill for consistent reuse; leave the one-off task as an unstructured session.
Recurring workflows and one-off tasks should be built identically, since the underlying tool used to complete either one is the same.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined rollup as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; B over-engineers the one-off task; D ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The compliance team wants documented evidence of who accessed what production and quality data through the system, and when, across all rollout sites.

choices.text: Access logging is optional if the system already has role-based permissions configured against a fixed access schema, since permissions alone constrain who can act.
Audit logging can be added later without architectural impact, once the compliance team formally requests the specific evidence it needs.

Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity validation, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an implicit byproduct of normal operation.
Only failed access attempts need to be logged in a structured format, since successful, authorized access doesn't carry the same compliance risk.

questions.explanation: Access control and audit logging need to be explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an incidental byproduct. A, B, and D each understate what compliance-grade audit evidence actually requires.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The steering committee for this rollout includes plant operations, legal/compliance, and engineering stakeholders across multiple countries with different priorities and vocabularies.

choices.text: Communicate only with the engineering stakeholders directly, since they'll relay the relevant information to operations and legal as needed.
Use identical technical documentation for all three audiences to save effort, trusting each group to extract what matters to them.
Tailor architectural communication to each audience — tradeoffs framed in terms operations and legal stakeholders can evaluate against their own priorities, not just engineering metrics.
Skip stakeholder communication entirely until the system is fully built and ready to demonstrate across every plant site.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by operations, legal, and engineering audiences alike. A, B, and D each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: Midway through the rollout, requirements shift meaningfully at several plants based on a new regional safety-certification standard.

choices.text: Treat this as normal lifecycle management — re-engage discovery for the affected scope, communicate the tradeoff to stakeholders, and adjust design and timeline accordingly.
Refuse to incorporate the change, since the original requirements were already validated and agreed upon before the new certification standard appeared.
Incorporate the change silently without informing stakeholders of its impact on scope, design, or the rollout timeline.
Restart the entire rollout from scratch across every plant and country, regardless of how narrow the new regional certification standard's actual scope of impact turns out to be.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally-driven requirements shift. B and C mishandle a real change; D disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: After the initial rollout, the architect's involvement is discussed as ending at handoff to each plant's local operations team.

choices.text: This is the correct lifecycle model; monitoring and iteration afterward are entirely the local operations teams' responsibility from that point on, with no further architectural input expected.
Lifecycle responsibility ends once the contract is signed, regardless of what happens to the system during actual production operation.
Monitoring is only necessary if a major incident occurs, so no ongoing architectural involvement is needed absent a specific failure.
Lifecycle management includes monitoring and iteration based on production signal as part of the architect's ongoing responsibility, not just discovery through handoff.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle management extends through monitoring and iteration based on production signal, not just through handoff. A, B, and C all end architectural responsibility earlier than the lifecycle model calls for.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: Documentation for this system currently lists final configuration values (model tier, retry settings, thresholds) with no explanation of why each was chosen.

choices.text: This level of documentation is sufficient, since the final configuration values — model tier, retry settings, thresholds — are all a future team would ever actually need to extend the system safely.
Documentation should also capture the "why" behind key decisions — compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning — so a future team can safely extend the system without re-deriving that context.
Documenting reasoning is unnecessary overhead across a multi-site rollout, since configuration values alone already fully describe the system's behavior.
Only the original architect should ever be allowed to modify the system going forward, which makes further documentation effectively moot.

questions.explanation: Capturing the "why" (compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning) alongside the "what" is what lets a future team safely extend the system, especially across a multi-site rollout. A, C, and D all leave that reasoning undocumented and effectively lost.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: The plant-engineering team wants Claude Code to help with routine tasks (drafting maintenance documentation, exploring an unfamiliar control-system module) but is unsure where it actually saves meaningful time versus adding review overhead.

choices.text: Assume AI-assisted tooling always saves time on every task category by default, since Claude Code is generally faster than manual work.
Mandate Claude Code usage for all tasks regardless of measured benefit, since broad adoption alone justifies the tooling investment.

Evaluate specific task categories for genuine friction reduction — e.g., repetitive documentation drafting, codebase exploration — versus cases where review overhead may exceed time saved, rather than assuming a blanket benefit.
Ban Claude Code for all documentation tasks without evaluation, since drafting maintenance documentation is inherently a low-value use case.

questions.explanation: Evaluating specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead gives an evidence-based answer instead of assuming a blanket benefit either way. A and B over-assume benefit; D forecloses potential benefit without evaluation.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Lifecycle Management and Enablement for a Global Manufacturing Rollout
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Industrial Group is rolling out a Claude-powered quality-flagging system on production lines and Claude Code for a 40-person plant-engineering team, across multiple countries. You are responsible for governance, compliance, and developer enablement across the rollout's lifecycle.
questions.prompt: A recurring operational issue is that different engineers across plants debug similar Claude Code integration failures independently, each re-deriving the same integration-layer-versus-model-output triage process.

choices.text: This is an acceptable ongoing inefficiency with no real architectural fix, since each plant's integration setup differs slightly anyway.
Document the triage process — distinguishing integration-layer from model-output failures — as shared operational knowledge across plants.
Restrict debugging of Claude Code integration failures to a single designated engineer who handles every plant's issues personally.

The issue can only be resolved by switching every plant to a different tool entirely, since Claude Code integration failures are inherently and permanently harder to triage than ordinary software bugs.

questions.explanation: Documenting the shared triage process turns individually re-derived knowledge into reusable operational knowledge, directly addressing the redundant-effort problem described. A accepts avoidable inefficiency; C and D propose disproportionate structural changes instead of the straightforward documentation fix. --- *End of Practice Exam 6.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: Discovery with Meridian's litigation-support leadership reveals the actual goal: processing 5x the current document-review volume during peak discovery windows, using the same review team size and without increasing average per-document review time.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around transformation, since leadership will want a novel-capability story even though discovery pointed at headcount and cycle time instead.
Frame the architecture around efficiency and build success metrics around review throughput per reviewer.
Frame the architecture around risk reduction, since litigation work is inherently risk-sensitive regardless of the stated volume goal.
Skip framing around any value pillar; a working system will justify itself to the partners without a named story.

questions.explanation: The stated goal (more volume, same headcount, unchanged review time) is an efficiency problem, so naming that pillar shapes both the architecture and its metrics. A assumes a transformation narrative that discovery didn't actually support; C substitutes a different pillar than the one leadership named; D skips framing instead of using what discovery surfaced.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: Document-review steps vary by document type, by findings from earlier documents in the same custodian's collection, and by whether a privilege flag was already raised — the right next step isn't knowable in advance.

choices.text: A fixed workflow, since document review is a well-established process with predictable steps.
An augmented LLM pattern, since one enhanced call with retrieval can resolve any document-review question in a single pass without further steps.
An agentic pattern, since the right next step depends on document type and on findings discovered earlier in the same collection.
Whichever pattern the review team already knows, since the four patterns are functionally interchangeable in practice.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by document type and depend on findings discovered along the way are the defining case for an agentic pattern. A assumes a predictability the scenario lacks; B undersells the orchestration a single enhanced call can't provide here; D treats genuinely different patterns as interchangeable.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to specialized subagents: document classification, privilege screening, relevance tagging, and production formatting.

choices.text: Let each subagent pass its output directly to whichever subagent needs it next, skipping the coordinator entirely to save a hop.
Merge all four responsibilities into a single subagent, since combining them removes coordination overhead entirely.
Route all inter-subagent communication through the coordinator, preserving observability and consistent error handling.
Allow direct subagent-to-subagent communication, but require each subagent to log its own traffic separately.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability and consistent error handling. A and D sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; B discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents in the first place.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: Every subagent performs its assigned task correctly, but the coordinator's decomposition routes only email and standard office documents through the pipeline — text messages and voicemail transcripts are never assigned to any subagent and silently skip review entirely.

choices.text: Add a fifth subagent purely to catch document formats the other four don't recognize.
Instruct the existing subagents, via prompt, to flag any document type they don't recognize as their own.
Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers every document format in the collection.
Expand every subagent's tool access so each one can process any document type it happens to receive.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while whole document formats are never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. A, B, and D all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap in the coordinator's routing.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. questions.prompt: The design must align the technical architecture to a specific business value pillar the firm's leadership actually cares about, rather than a generic "we added AI to document review" narrative.

choices.text: Name a pillar such as efficiency, risk reduction, cost, or defensibility, and let that choice drive both the architecture and its metrics.
Any AI-assisted review process inherently demonstrates transformation, so no separate framing conversation with leadership is required.
Business value pillars are a business-development concern the architecture team can leave to the partners entirely.
Select the pillar after launch, based on whichever production metric happens to look best at the time.

questions.explanation: Business value pillars (efficiency, risk reduction, cost, defensibility) give both the architecture and its metrics a clear anchor. B, C, and D all skip, misassign, or defer this framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: Discovery interviews with the firm's contract reviewers and paralegals repeatedly surface anxiety that the platform will eliminate their roles.

choices.text: Disregard the sentiment in the architecture conversation, since it isn't a stated technical requirement from leadership.
Proceed with the technical design as planned and let a separate change-management effort handle morale, with zero architectural input.
Recommend cancelling the project on the basis of the sentiment alone, without weighing it against the stated volume goal.
Treat the sentiment as a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints go.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment is a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter — it's discovery input, not noise to ignore. A and B treat it as out of scope for the architecture; C overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing it against the stated volume goal.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm

The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: A partner asks why the privilege-screening subagent runs on a higher-capability, higher-cost model tier than the document-classification subagent.

choices.text: Explain that privilege calls carry high error cost and need deeper reasoning, which justifies the added cost and latency over the simpler classification task.
Respond that the higher tier is used "because privilege is important," and move on without further detail.
Avoid answering directly, since partners aren't expected to understand technical tier decisions.
Standardize both subagents on one tier for simplicity, since tier matching mostly matters at far higher volume than this.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. B and C withhold the reasoning stakeholders actually need; D removes a deliberate, justified difference for a simplicity that doesn't hold up at the described error stakes.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: The current design produces a final privilege/relevance recommendation with no mechanism to capture attorney overrides or downstream case outcomes for future improvement.

choices.text: This is acceptable for now, since the initial classification logic already reflects current review-team best practice.
Add a feedback loop, as a first-class architectural component, that captures attorney overrides and case outcomes for improving the system after launch.
Feedback loops are a data-science concern that has no bearing on the architecture itself.
Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase, with no hooks designed into the current build.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures attorney overrides and outcomes as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve after deployment. A, C, and D all treat that component as optional, someone else's concern, or something to defer indefinitely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: For a narrower need, the firm wants a single enhanced call — with retrieval over the firm's internal case-law and precedent database — to answer straightforward "has this privilege argument been raised before in this matter" questions, without multi-step autonomous orchestration.

choices.text: This requires a full multi-agent architecture regardless of how narrow the underlying task actually is.
This can't be built with Claude, since retrieval-augmented lookups always need autonomous agent behavior in order to function.
This requires a fixed, structured workflow of at least four sequential steps, matching the platform's other pipelines.
An augmented LLM pattern — a single call enhanced with retrieval — fits this narrower need without agentic overhead.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with retrieval, without multi-step autonomous orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern is for. A and C over-engineer a simple augmentation need by importing structure from the platform's other workflows; B is factually wrong about what the pattern requires.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. questions.prompt: The document-classification subagent's toolset has grown to include tools for tasks like billing-code lookup and client-invoice generation, unrelated to classification.

choices.text: This carries no architectural downside as long as the subagent's system prompt stays well-structured.
More tools always increase a subagent's flexibility, so the growing toolset should be encouraged as the platform expands.
This capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability; remove or relocate the unrelated tools.
The correct fix is to increase the subagent's context window rather than reconsider its toolset.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows — the fix is removing or relocating them, not writing around it. A and B ignore this real degradation; D reaches for the wrong lever, since the problem is toolset scope, not context capacity.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: The coordinator currently runs document classification, then privilege screening, then relevance tagging, then production formatting strictly in sequence, even though privilege screening and relevance tagging have no dependency on each other's output.

choices.text: Run privilege screening and relevance tagging as independent, parallel calls once classification finishes.
Sequential processing across all four stages is required to preserve an admissible, defensible audit trail for the matter.
Parallelization of independent subagent calls isn't achievable within a coordinator/subagent architecture.
Combine privilege screening and relevance tagging into a single subagent to sidestep the sequencing question.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite (classification) completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. B and C misstate real constraints on the architecture; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: Firm leadership asks how the end-to-end architecture should be described to a steering committee of partners unfamiliar with the technical implementation.

choices.text: Present only the model names and per-document token costs, since those are the numbers leadership asks about first.
Present the complete technical architecture diagram, including subagent prompts and tool schemas, with no simplification for the audience.
Describe input → processing → output → feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against defensibility and throughput goals.
Skip a high-level description and move directly into a live system demo, letting the interface speak for itself.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A gives too little of the relevant detail; B gives too much of the wrong kind of detail; D skips the communication need entirely in favor of a demo.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: A competing vendor proposes a single generalist agent holding every tool (classification, privilege logic, relevance tagging, production formatting) instead of a coordinator with specialized subagents.

choices.text: A single generalist agent scales better as the number of tools grows, since it avoids inter-agent coordination overhead.
Specialized subagents are strictly a cost-increasing choice, since running several narrow agents costs more than one broad one.
There is no meaningful architectural difference between the two approaches once both use the same underlying model.
A single agent holding every tool is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than narrower subagents.

questions.explanation: A single generalist agent holding every tool and responsibility is more exposed to degraded tool-selection reliability than agents scoped to narrower roles — the core argument for specialization. A, B, and C understate or misstate this real architectural tradeoff.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: The platform must eventually support a new matter type (regulatory investigations with different privilege rules) the firm expects to take on next year, but detailed requirements aren't defined yet.

choices.text: Ignore future matter types entirely in the current design until firm requirements for regulatory investigations exist.
Build full support for regulatory-investigation privilege rules now, filling gaps in the undefined requirements with guesses.
Design current subagent boundaries with reasonable extensibility in mind, without over-building for speculative requirements.
Refuse to proceed with the current phase until next year's requirements are formally finalized by the firm.

questions.explanation: Reasonable extensibility without over-building for undefined future requirements balances current delivery against future flexibility. A ignores a known future need entirely; B wastes effort guessing at requirements that don't exist yet; D blocks current delivery over information that isn't available yet.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent E-Discovery Platform for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Discovery Partners, a litigation-support firm serving Am Law 100 clients, is building a Claude-powered e-discovery platform to review, tag, and produce documents for active litigation matters. The platform must classify documents for relevance, screen for attorney-client privilege, and route borderline calls to reviewing attorneys. You are the architect responsible for the multi-agent design and for running discovery with the firm's litigation-support leadership.
questions.prompt: Firm leadership wants documentation they can hand to a new engineering vendor in a year, who will extend the platform without the original architect present.

choices.text: Document only the final configuration values, since a well-organized implementation is otherwise self-explanatory.
Document the reasoning behind key decisions — pattern choices, subagent boundaries, tier selections — not just the final values, so a future vendor isn't left re-deriving that context from scratch.
Rely on the original architect remaining reachable indefinitely instead of writing anything down.
Documentation is unnecessary as long as the code and prompts themselves stay well-organized.

questions.explanation: Documenting the reasoning behind key decisions, not just final values, is what lets a future team safely extend the system without the original architect present. A, C, and D all leave the actual knowledge-transfer gap unaddressed.
