questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only flag precision and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Precision alone is sufficient, since flagging suspicious transactions accurately is the fraud-triage system's stated primary purpose.
Define evaluation metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security as first-class metrics — flagging fraud well isn't enough if the system is too slow, expensive, or unsafe.
Latency and cost are purely operations concerns, unrelated to how the fraud-detection evaluation strategy itself should be designed.

Safety and security metrics are only relevant for systems operating in explicitly regulated industries, and a payments fraud-triage system handling live transactions doesn't need them defined as first-class metrics at all.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if it flags fraud well. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past transactions.

choices.text: A single automated evaluation method is sufficient for any production system, regardless of how nuanced its failure modes are.
Replace the automated checks entirely with only human review, since automation can't capture nuanced judgment calls.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely, treating a bigger fixed dataset as the sole lever for improving evaluation coverage.

Use mixed methodologies — automated eval for scale, human review for nuanced judgment calls, and adversarial/edge-case testing for safety-relevant paths — since no single method covers every failure mode.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and C each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new triage-scoring prompt improves flag quality before rolling it out to all traffic.

choices.text: Roll out the new prompt to all traffic immediately and monitor informally for problems after the fact.
Change the prompt and the model tier at the same time, to maximize the potential improvement from both changes in a single rollout rather than testing them separately.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any difference can be attributed to that one change.
Skip testing entirely, since prompt changes are inherently low-risk and rarely affect flag quality.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; D dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: A flagged transaction was wrongly cleared as legitimate. Investigation shows the underlying transaction-history data was retrieved correctly, and the model's response paraphrased it inaccurately.

choices.text: This is best characterized as a prompt/generation issue (inaccurate paraphrasing of correctly retrieved data), which calls for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.
This is a retrieval problem, so the fix should focus on the indexing pipeline that surfaced the transaction history, even though the investigation found the retrieved data itself was accurate.
This can't be diagnosed at all without retraining the underlying model from scratch on new data.
This is a model mismatch requiring a switch to a different model tier, regardless of what the specific failure actually was.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. B and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; C avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled transaction-history database migration, the system starts flagging an elevated rate of clean transactions as fraud, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider, even though nothing in the validation logs points to a model-side change.
Investigate the retrieval/indexing layer first, since the regression is tied specifically to the data migration event with model version and average latency unchanged.
Suspect a temperature setting change, since the flagging behavior changed right after the migration.
Suspect the context window shrank, even though window size has no bearing on how deterministic the model's flagging output is.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data migration event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, C, and D would not specifically correlate with a transaction-history migration.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency of fraud triage but is worried about hurting recall, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Cost, latency, and accuracy should each be optimized independently, one at a time and in isolation, since combining all three into a single joint tradeoff decision only overcomplicates an already difficult recall-versus-cost analysis.
Optimize cost/latency/accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget — the cheapest configuration that fails the recall bar isn't a win.
Accuracy should always be maximized regardless of what that does to cost or latency, since fraud detection is the priority.
This tradeoff can't be measured with the data available; it can only be guessed at until more data accumulates.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "recall at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the recall bar. A and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring currently reports only an overall weekly average precision score.

choices.text: A single aggregate weekly average is sufficient for production monitoring, regardless of what a specific merchant category or transaction type happening underneath it might actually be hiding.
Monitoring should track only cost, since accuracy is already captured by the separate, structured eval suite.
Monitoring should surface drift and outliers — a per-merchant or per-transaction-type breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a failing segment.
Weekly granularity is always sufficient regardless of how the system's behavior actually changes day to day.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. A and D accept a monitoring blind spot; B drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting manual review of flagged transactions by 70%, citing a 98% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Segment accuracy by merchant category and transaction type before cutting review, since an aggregate figure can mask a badly underperforming segment.
Proceed with the 70% review cut based on the 98% aggregate figure alone, trusting that number to reflect real performance.
Aggregate accuracy is, by definition, representative of how every individual merchant or transaction segment is performing underneath it.
Human review should never be reduced under any circumstances, regardless of what a segmented accuracy analysis eventually shows about risk concentration.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by merchant category and transaction type before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new triage model improves flag precision, but the team hasn't checked whether it also changed the false-negative rate on sophisticated fraud patterns that should be escalated.

choices.text: Precision improvement alone is a sufficient signal to ship the change, without checking any other failure mode.
False-negative escalation behavior isn't something evaluation can measure at all, so it isn't worth specifically checking before a change ships to production traffic.
Check the escalation-related failure mode specifically before shipping — an isolated precision gain could be masking missed sophisticated fraud.
Ship the change and monitor informally after the fact, instead of testing the escalation behavior beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated precision improvement could mask a worsened escalation failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and D ship without adequate testing; B incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of flagged transactions are technically correctly classified but investigators rate the accompanying explanation as unhelpful.

choices.text: Assume the accuracy metric itself is broken and discard it, since it doesn't reflect what investigators are reporting.

Increase the model's capability tier across the board, on the assumption that a higher-capability model will always produce more highly rated explanations regardless of what investigators actually found unhelpful.
Ignore investigator ratings entirely and rely on the accuracy metric's validation results alone as the sole quality signal.

Investigate a dimension beyond factual accuracy — e.g., clarity, completeness, or actionability of the explanation — since "correct but unhelpful" points at a quality dimension the current eval doesn't measure.

questions.explanation: "Correct but unhelpful" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (clarity, completeness, actionability) rather than a broken accuracy metric. A and C discard a working, differently-scoped metric; B assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends the full transaction history plus a large static fraud-policy document on every turn of multi-turn investigator conversations.

choices.text: Apply prompt caching to the static fraud-policy document and trim or summarize older conversation turns to reduce redundant token cost.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost, without changing what's resent unchanged on every single turn.
Remove the fraud-policy document from the prompt entirely to save tokens, even on turns where the policy is directly relevant.
Full transaction history is always required on every turn, so there's no optimization opportunity here worth pursuing.

questions.explanation: Caching the static fraud-policy document and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. D denies an obvious lever; C removes needed content; B is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the production system, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Raw logging at full volume is itself a sufficient observability strategy, as long as the logs are retained somewhere and nobody deletes them during a routine cleanup.
Reduce logging volume to save on storage cost, without making any other change to how it's structured.
Observability requires no particular structure, as long as the underlying data is retained somewhere for later use.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged failure categories, segment-level quality metrics — since raw logs at volume aren't reviewable on their own.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and C accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a quality regression was caused by a recent prompt change, a recent model version change, or a fraud-policy document update — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: Assume the most recent of the three changes is always the one responsible for the regression, without testing that assumption against the prompt or fraud-policy changes shipped the same week.
Attribution is impossible once multiple changes have shipped in the same week, so the question isn't worth pursuing.
This is why changes should be tested and rolled out one variable at a time — with three simultaneous changes, attribution requires isolating each independently.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which one, if any, actually caused the regression.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and D guess without evidence; B gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a triage-explanation output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for inherently non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check for required content/structure rather than exact text.
The model is malfunctioning and needs to be retrained before the eval can be trusted again.
The reference string needs to be made longer, and its exact-match validation left as-is, so more of the output matches it.
The eval's threshold for what counts as a pass needs to be loosened until the intermittent failures stop appearing.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. B and D misdiagnose model behavior as broken; C doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Optimization of a Fraud-Detection Triage System
questions.scenario_context: A Claude-powered system at Vantage Payments flags suspicious transactions for human investigator review. It's been in production for eight months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the fraud-triage system is, to track over time.

choices.text: A single aggregate metric can be a useful top-line indicator, but should be paired with segment-level and multi-dimensional detail so a healthy top-line number doesn't mask a failing area.
Use flag precision alone as the single number, since that's the system's stated primary purpose.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric at all, regardless of how clearly leadership has asked for one.

A single number is always fully achievable and sufficient for representing any system's evaluation needs, regardless of how many distinct dimensions like latency, cost, and safety actually feed into it.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. B and D oversimplify to a single lossy number; C refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The architecture team is finalizing data flow, retention, and access-logging design in the final week before launch, after core application logic is already built.

choices.text: This sequencing carries no real risk, since data-minimization, retention, and access-control requirements can always be layered on cleanly in the final week without touching anything already built.
Compliance only affects legal documentation and contracts, not the system's underlying technical architecture.
HIPAA, not GDPR, is the relevant regulatory regime for a retail bank operating inside the EU.
GDPR-driven data-minimization, retention, and access-control requirements can force structural changes that are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the start.

questions.explanation: GDPR-driven requirements can force structural changes that are far costlier to retrofit after core logic is built than to design in from the start. A and B understate real architectural impact; C misidentifies the applicable regulatory regime.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: A team proposes requiring human approval on every single output the customer-facing system produces, framing it as the safest governance posture.

choices.text: Maximal human review on every single output is always the correct default posture for a banking AI system, regardless of cost.
Blanket human-in-the-loop on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should be targeted at high error-cost or genuinely judgment-requiring decisions rather than applied universally.
Human reviewers are categorically less accurate than the model on every task, making review counterproductive across the board.
This universal-review approach is required by GDPR regardless of the error cost or judgment involved in a given output.

questions.explanation: Blanket human review on every output defeats much of the system's value; HITL should target high error-cost or judgment-requiring decisions specifically. A and C overstate the universal safety case for maximal review; D misattributes this requirement to GDPR, which doesn't mandate it universally.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The system must identify and mitigate standard LLM risks — hallucination, prompt injection from customer-submitted free text, and inconsistent output — as part of its design.

choices.text: These risks only need to be addressed reactively, once each one is actually observed happening in live production traffic, rather than designed against ahead of the initial customer-facing launch date.
These three risks are considered exclusive to non-banking use cases and therefore don't meaningfully apply to a regulated financial system.
A single generic guardrail, applied once across the board, addresses hallucination, prompt injection, and inconsistent output equally well without any task-specific tuning.
Design mitigations for each known failure mode up front — grounding for hallucination, isolation for injection, validation for consistency — rather than as a reactive afterthought.

questions.explanation: Designing mitigations for each known failure mode (grounding for hallucination, isolation/guardrails for injection, validation for consistency) up front is the architecture-first approach the domain calls for. A defers to a reactive posture; C assumes one guardrail covers distinct risk types; B is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance team asks whether the system's credit-related outputs could produce disparate outcomes across different demographic groups.

choices.text: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns — evaluate whether training/eval data reflects the served population rather than assuming disparate impact is absent.
This isn't an architectural concern at all; it belongs entirely to legal and compliance review conducted after the system has already launched.
Disparate impact is impossible in an LLM-based system by construction, regardless of what data it was trained or evaluated on or how closely that data reflects the population actually served.
This concern only applies to systems making final, legally binding credit decisions, not to an assistive system that merely supports representatives.

questions.explanation: Bias, fairness, and transparency are architecture concerns requiring active measurement (data representativeness, disparate-impact checks), not an assumption of absence. B defers a design concern entirely to a later stage; C and D make unsupported blanket claims.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The engineering team's Claude Code usage is inconsistent — some engineers have team conventions applied automatically, others don't, and internal MCP server access varies by machine.

choices.text: Have each engineer individually troubleshoot their own local configuration, without any shared team-level standard to converge on.
Standardize CLAUDE.md hierarchy and shared MCP server configuration at the team level so behavior doesn't depend on individual local machine setup at all.
Restrict Claude Code usage to a single designated engineer, so configuration variance across the rest of the team simply stops mattering.
Accept the inconsistency as an unavoidable, permanent cost of adopting AI-assisted tooling across a team of engineers.

questions.explanation: Standardizing CLAUDE.md and shared MCP configuration at the team level directly fixes the described inconsistency, which stems from relying on individual local setup. A and D leave the systemic cause unaddressed; C sacrifices the tool's benefit for the rest of the team.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The team wants Claude Code-generated code changes in this banking context to go through the same review rigor as any other change to a regulated system.

choices.text: AI-assisted code should bypass standard review entirely, since Claude Code generated it directly and a human author would have needed the same review a hand-written change requires.
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply; Claude Code assisting with generation doesn't reduce the review rigor required for a regulated system.
Only a quick spot-check validation of the AI-generated portion is necessary, rather than the full review process.
Review requirements should be set lower for AI-generated code than for equivalent human-written code in the same system.

questions.explanation: Standard SDLC review rigor still applies regardless of whether Claude Code assisted with generation, especially in a regulated system. A, C, and D all propose reducing rigor specifically because AI was involved, which is the wrong direction for a regulated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: A production incident traces back to a Claude Code-generated data-handling change. The team can't immediately tell whether the bug is in the generated code logic or in how the surrounding system integrated it.

choices.text: Assume the bug is in the generated code without first investigating whether the integration layer is actually at fault.
Disable Claude Code for the team entirely, following any incident regardless of where the actual root cause turns out to be once the traces and logs are actually reviewed.
Triage the same way any incident is triaged — isolate whether the issue is in the integration layer or the model output — using traces and logs.
Roll back all recent Claude Code-assisted changes regardless of whether they're actually relevant to this incident.

questions.explanation: Standard incident triage — isolating integration-layer versus model/code-output failure via traces/logs — applies here just as it would to any other incident. A and D skip diagnosis; B is a disproportionate reaction that doesn't investigate the actual cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The engineering team wants a documented, repeatable workflow for a recurring task (generating a weekly GDPR data-subject-access-request summary report) versus a one-off exploratory coding task.

choices.text: Build both the recurring report and the one-off exploratory task as ad hoc, undocumented prompts each time either is needed.

Package the recurring, well-defined report workflow as a Skill for on-demand, consistent reuse; leave the one-off exploratory task as an unstructured session, since it doesn't need standing infrastructure.
Build both the recurring report and the one-off task as MCP servers, regardless of how often either one is actually reused.
Recurring, well-defined workflows and one-off exploratory tasks should always be built with identical structure.

questions.explanation: Packaging the recurring, well-defined report as a Skill matches its reuse profile; leaving the one-off exploratory task unstructured avoids unnecessary standing infrastructure. A under-serves the recurring task; C over-engineers the one-off task; D ignores that reuse profile should drive the choice.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The compliance team wants documented evidence of who accessed what customer data through the system and when.

choices.text: Access logging is optional as long as the system already enforces a role-based permission schema on who can reach which data.

Audit logging can always be layered on afterward without any architectural impact, once role-based permissions and the rest of the customer-data-handling system are already fully built and shipped to production.
Only failed access attempts need a structured log entry; successful, authorized access doesn't need one.
Design access-control and audit-logging as explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an implicit byproduct.

questions.explanation: Access control and audit logging need to be explicit architectural components satisfying identity, authorization, and monitoring requirements — not an incidental byproduct. A, B, and C each understate what compliance-grade audit evidence actually requires.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: The steering committee for this deployment includes compliance, risk, and engineering stakeholders with different priorities and vocabularies.

choices.text: Communicate only with the engineering stakeholders, trusting them to relay the relevant tradeoffs to compliance and risk.
Skip stakeholder communication until the system is fully built and ready for a single end-of-project readout.
Use identical technical documentation for all three audiences — compliance, risk, and engineering — to save preparation effort, trusting each group to extract what matters to them.
Tailor architectural communication to each audience — tradeoffs framed in terms compliance and risk stakeholders can evaluate against their own priorities.

questions.explanation: Tailoring communication to each stakeholder group's priorities and vocabulary is what makes architectural tradeoffs actually evaluable by compliance, risk, and engineering audiences alike. A, B, and C each fail to serve at least one audience's real information need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: Midway through the project, requirements shift meaningfully based on new EU regulatory guidance.

choices.text: Refuse to incorporate the new regulatory guidance, since requirements were already agreed upon and finalized earlier in the project timeline.
Incorporate the change silently, without informing any stakeholders that the project's scope or timeline impact has meaningfully shifted.
Treat this as a normal part of lifecycle management — re-engage discovery for the affected scope and communicate the tradeoff of the change to stakeholders.
Restart the entire project from scratch, regardless of how narrow the new guidance's actual scope turns out to be in practice.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging discovery for the affected scope and communicating the tradeoff of the change is standard lifecycle management for a legitimate, externally-driven requirements shift. A and B mishandle a real change; D disproportionately discards unaffected work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: After launch, the architect's involvement is discussed as ending at handoff to the operations team.

choices.text: This is the correct lifecycle model; once handoff to the operations team happens, ongoing monitoring and iteration based on production signal become entirely their responsibility going forward.
Lifecycle management includes monitoring and iteration based on production signal as part of the architect's ongoing responsibility, not just discovery through handoff.
Lifecycle responsibility ends once the contract with the operations team is signed, regardless of what happens in production afterward.
Monitoring is only necessary if a major incident actually occurs sometime after handoff; otherwise it can reasonably be skipped entirely.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle management extends through monitoring and iteration based on production signal, not just through handoff. A, C, and D all end architectural responsibility earlier than the lifecycle model calls for.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. You are responsible for governance, GDPR compliance, and stakeholder communication for the launch.
questions.prompt: Documentation for this system currently lists final configuration values (model tier, retry settings, thresholds) with no explanation of why each was chosen.

choices.text: Documentation should also capture the "why" behind key decisions — compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning — not just the final configuration values.

This level of documentation is already sufficient, since the final configuration values — model tier, retry settings, thresholds — are all a future team would ever realistically need to safely extend the system.
Documenting the reasoning behind each decision is unnecessary overhead in an already heavily regulated environment.
Only the original architect should ever be allowed to modify the system, which makes documentation effectively moot.

questions.explanation: Capturing the "why" (compliance drivers, tradeoff reasoning) alongside the "what" is what lets a future team safely extend the system, especially in a regulated context. B, C, and D all leave that reasoning undocumented and effectively lost.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Governance and Stakeholder Communication for a Banking GDPR Deployment
questions.scenario_context: Nordbank, an EU retail bank, is deploying a Claude-powered system that assists customer-service representatives and supports internal credit-related workflows, alongside a small engineering team using Claude Code internally. questions.prompt: The engineering team wants Claude Code to help with routine tasks (drafting documentation, exploring an unfamiliar module) but is unsure where it actually saves meaningful time versus adding review overhead.

choices.text: Assume AI-assisted tooling always saves meaningful time on every task category, by default, without measuring documentation drafting or codebase exploration specifically.
Evaluate specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus cases where review overhead may exceed time saved, rather than assuming a blanket benefit.
Mandate Claude Code usage for every task category regardless of any measured benefit or added review overhead.
Ban Claude Code for all structured documentation tasks outright, without evaluating whether it actually reduces friction on repetitive drafting work.

questions.explanation: Evaluating specific task categories for genuine friction reduction versus added review overhead gives an evidence-based answer instead of assuming a blanket benefit either way. A and C over-assume benefit; D forecloses potential benefit without evaluation.

You are the architect leading discovery and design.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the real business driver is reducing carrier detention and demurrage fees by 30%, not adding capabilities the current process lacks.

choices.text: Frame the rollout around transformation, arguing new automated capability justifies the investment even though discovery pointed at a cost driver.
Frame the rollout around throughput and efficiency gains exclusively, since faster cycle times are easier to demonstrate than fee reduction.
Skip formal pillar framing and let the detention-fee savings show up in the executive dashboard after go-live.
Frame around cost reduction, anchoring both the architecture and success metrics on detention/demurrage fee reduction.

questions.explanation: Discovery pointed to a cost driver (detention/demurrage fees), so the architecture and metrics should be anchored on cost reduction. A and B reach for a different pillar than what discovery found; C skips framing that keeps the project aligned to real value.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Supply-Chain and Logistics Orchestration Platform

You are the architect leading discovery and design.
questions.prompt: Procurement, mode selection, and exception handling each require different steps depending on carrier responses, inventory position, and disruptions discovered mid-shipment.

choices.text: Use an agentic pattern, since the right sequence of procurement, mode-selection, and exception steps varies by shipment and depends on intermediate findings.
Use a fixed workflow with a predetermined step order, since freight logistics across carriers is standardized enough that branching adds needless complexity.
Use a single augmented LLM call with retrieval and tools, since one well-prompted call can absorb procurement, routing, and exception handling together.
Pick whichever pattern prototypes fastest this sprint, since procurement, routing, and exception handling are functionally interchangeable workloads.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by shipment and depend on intermediate findings (carrier responses, disruptions) are the defining case for an agentic pattern. B assumes a predictability the scenario lacks; C undersells the orchestration needed; D treats genuinely different patterns as interchangeable.

You are the architect leading discovery and design.
questions.prompt: The design has a coordinator delegating to subagents (procurement, routing, exception-handling, customs-compliance). Every subagent works correctly, but shipments requiring both a customs hold and a carrier substitution are never routed to any subagent — they fall through silently.

choices.text: Add a fifth "edge case" subagent whose whole job is catching any shipment that none of the four existing specialists recognize as belonging to their own domain.
Instruct each subagent to flag any shipment whose details look unfamiliar, so the coordinator can retry routing.
Broaden every subagent's tool access so any of the four can pick up a compound customs-plus-substitution case if it slips through.
Fix the coordinator's decomposition to explicitly cover compound cases like simultaneous holds and substitutions.

questions.explanation: Whole compound case categories never being routed at all is a coordinator decomposition gap, not a subagent performance issue. A, B, and C all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap in the coordinator's routing logic.

Treat any automated system as inherently demonstrating transformation, since replacing manual steps with AI is transformation by definition.
Treat business value pillars as a sales and marketing concern that architecture doesn't need to reference.
Defer picking a pillar until after launch, then choose whichever benefit turned out easiest to report to leadership.

questions.explanation: Naming a specific pillar (efficiency, cost, transformation, SLA) gives both architecture and metrics a clear anchor. B, C, and D each skip or defer that framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

Proceed with the design as planned and hand the sentiment entirely to a separate change-management workstream later.
Recommend shelving the project based on dispatcher pushback alone, without weighing the cost case discovery already established for the rollout.
Treat the sentiment as a real implicit constraint that shapes rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter most.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment from dispatchers is a real implicit constraint shaping rollout sequencing and HITL placement, not noise to dismiss. A and B treat it as out of scope; C overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing the cost case already established.

Avoid the tier question altogether, on the assumption that stakeholders don't need or want any technical detail.
Explain the tradeoff explicitly — exception handling needs deeper reasoning over disruptive events, justifying its cost, while procurement is routine.
Use the same tier everywhere for simplicity, arguing that per-task tier tuning isn't worth the ongoing configuration and monitoring overhead it adds.

Add a feedback loop capturing dispatcher overrides and delivery outcomes as a first-class architectural component.
Treat feedback loops as a data-science team's concern, outside the scope of the architecture being reviewed here.
Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase, with no hooks or schema reserved for it in the current design.

questions.explanation: A first-class feedback loop capturing dispatcher overrides and outcomes is what lets the system improve post-deployment. A, C, and D each treat this component as optional, someone else's job, or a someday concern.

Use an augmented LLM pattern — a single call enhanced with retrieval and tools — which fits this simpler augmentation need.
Require a fixed workflow with at least five sequential steps, even though the request is a single lookup.
Say this can't be built with Claude at all, since it involves no autonomous multi-step agent behavior.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with retrieval, without multi-step orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern serves. A and C over-engineer a simple augmentation need; D is factually wrong.

Treat more tools as always improving flexibility, and actively encourage adding further unrelated capabilities.
Increase the subagent's context window, on the theory that a bigger window offsets a larger, less-structured tool list.
Remove or relocate the unrelated tools, since this capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows. A and B ignore this real degradation; C treats a bigger context window as a substitute for fixing the actual selection problem.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. You are the architect leading discovery and design.
questions.prompt: The coordinator currently processes each shipment sequentially through procurement, routing, exception-check, and customs-check, even though routing and customs-check have no dependency on each other's output.

Run routing and customs-check as independent, parallel subagent calls once procurement completes.
Say true parallelization isn't possible once a coordinator delegates to specialized subagents.
Merge routing and customs-check into one subagent so the sequencing question never has to be answered.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no shared dependency can run in parallel once their prerequisite (procurement) completes, cutting latency without sacrificing correctness. A and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. Describe input, processing, output, and the feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against business outcomes.
Present the full technical architecture diagram exactly as built, including the raw system prompt text, with no simplification.
Skip the high-level description entirely and move straight into a live implementation demo.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A is insufficient detail, C is too much of the wrong kind, and D skips the communication need entirely.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. Say there's no meaningful architectural difference between a generalist agent and specialized subagents.
Say a single agent holding every tool is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than scoped subagents.
Say specialized subagents are strictly a cost-increasing choice with no reliability benefit over one agent.

questions.explanation: A single generalist agent holding every tool and responsibility is more exposed to degraded tool-selection reliability than agents scoped to narrower roles. A, B, and D understate or deny this real architectural tradeoff.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Systems, a mid-market logistics provider, wants to modernize its order-to-delivery pipeline — carrier-capacity procurement, route/mode selection, in-transit exception handling, and customs/compliance checks — using a Claude-powered multi-agent architecture. Design current decomposition with reasonable extensibility, without over-building for requirements that aren't defined yet.
Build full intermodal-rail support now, inventing requirements Meridian hasn't specified yet.
Refuse to proceed with the current phase at all until next year's full intermodal-rail requirements are finalized and signed off.

questions.explanation: Reasonable extensibility without over-building for undefined future requirements balances current delivery against future flexibility. A ignores a known future need; C wastes effort guessing; D blocks current delivery unnecessarily.

Plan for the original architect to remain reachable indefinitely, instead of writing anything down.
Treat documentation as unnecessary as long as the codebase itself stays well-organized.

Quietly build staffing-schedule automation too, so no stakeholder ends up disappointed at launch.
Ignore the misunderstanding, since staffing automation was never written into the original requirements document.
Cancel the current project until every stakeholder's expectations are fully unified.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Most attorney queries are moderately complex research questions; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many cases, and a small fraction are simple citation lookups.

choices.text: Route by difficulty — a fast tier for citation lookups, a balanced tier for typical research, and a higher-capability tier with extended thinking for deep multi-case reasoning.
Always use the highest-capability tier, to guarantee quality on every single question regardless of its actual difficulty.
Use one fixed model tier for every question, regardless of whether it's a lookup or a multi-case synthesis.
Always use the fastest, cheapest tier, accepting the quality loss on the deep multi-case questions.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex research questions. B and D ignore fit-to-task; C sacrifices quality on the cases that need capability most.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same long system prompt (jurisdiction rules, citation style, formatting requirements) followed by retrieved case excerpts that vary per query.

choices.text: Say prompt ordering doesn't affect cost or latency for a retrieval-heavy legal research workload.
Place the stable system prompt first with caching enabled, and the varying retrieved excerpts after it.
Put the retrieved excerpts before the system prompt, since they're the content most relevant to the specific attorney query.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt on each turn.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The corpus mixes long-form judicial opinions with short structured data (a table of statute citations and effective dates).

choices.text: Use one chunking strategy tuned for long-form opinions and apply it to the short structured statute table too.
Match chunking and indexing strategy to each data shape, since one strategy tuned for opinions degrades retrieval for structured records.
Exclude the structured statute-citation table from retrieval entirely, keeping only long-form opinions indexed.
Use the largest possible chunk size everywhere, to avoid maintaining two separate chunking strategies.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and D ignore this mismatch; C discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorney queries range from exact lookups ("cite for Smith v. Jones") to conceptual questions ("how has the reasonable-reliance standard evolved across circuits").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search, ignoring the structured citation metadata, for both exact lookups and conceptual questions.
Use only structured or metadata filtering, for both exact citation lookups and open-ended conceptual questions.
Match retrieval to query pattern: metadata filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where both matter.
Treat query pattern as irrelevant to which retrieval approach is the right fit for a given attorney question.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and B force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Attorneys need citations that reliably map each legal claim to a specific case and pincite, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Require structured output pairing each claim with its case, reporter citation, and pincite, so mapping survives synthesis.
Ask the model, in prose only, to "always cite sources," with no schema or field structure behind the instruction.
Add citations after drafting, by searching afterward for a plausible case to attach to each already-written claim.
Append a general bibliography of consulted cases at the end, without tying any specific claim to a specific source.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. B, C, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: Two retrieved cases disagree on how a particular statute of limitations is tolled — likely because they're from different circuits with different precedent.

choices.text: Average the two circuits' tolling positions together and present a single blended rule to the attorney.
Omit the tolling analysis from the answer entirely, since the two retrieved cases disagree with each other.
Always prefer whichever of the two conflicting cases the retrieval system happened to return first.
Present both positions explicitly, attributed to their respective circuits, rather than blending or silently picking one.

questions.explanation: Presenting both positions with attribution preserves the actual information for the attorney rather than resolving a genuine jurisdictional conflict arbitrarily. A, B, and C all discard or obscure a real disagreement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with citation fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Repeat the "always output valid JSON" instruction more emphatically, assuming the model's structured output is deterministic once phrased right.
Increase max_tokens, on the theory that more room fixes a preamble the model keeps generating before the JSON.
Use tool-use or schema-constrained output so structure is enforced by the API mechanism, not requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip any leading text that appears before the first curly brace.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and D are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; B doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform needs to connect to a proprietary internal brief bank, exposing search and retrieval capabilities to multiple different internal Claude-powered tools beyond just this research platform.

choices.text: Hard-code the brief-bank integration into this one research platform's application code only.
Paste the entire proprietary brief bank into every prompt that might need to reference it.
Build an MCP server exposing brief-bank operations as tools/resources, reusable across the internal tools.
Require each internal tool that needs the brief bank to reimplement its own separate integration and authentication layer independently.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. A, B, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates between exposing the full case-law catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Load the full case-law catalog into every prompt up front, on the theory that completeness always wins.
Treat context cost as roughly the same either way, since loading the full catalog and querying it on demand end up costing about the same per query.
Never expose the catalog to the agent in any form, forcing attorneys to search it manually outside Claude.
Use progressive discovery, querying a catalog resource as needed, which scales better as the corpus grows.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with corpus growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. A and B ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; C removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: An attorney asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several retrieved opinions before concluding on a multi-factor test.

choices.text: Use chain-of-thought prompting, letting the model reason step by step across the retrieved opinions before concluding.
Use zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance, since it performs equally well on any multi-document synthesis task.
Treat chain-of-thought prompting as useful only for coding tasks, not for legal multi-factor analysis.
Say the model can't reason across multiple documents no matter which prompting approach is used.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning across a multi-factor test. B, C, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, jurisdiction disclaimers, formatting rules) across several different attorney-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Duplicate the citation-format and disclaimer fragments into each attorney-facing feature's prompt independently.
Use modular, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — distinct from caching's cost/latency role or Skills' capability packaging.
Treat modular prompt fragments as just another name for prompt caching, since both involve reusing prompt content.
Say standardization across features isn't something prompt design can achieve at all.

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. A reintroduces duplication; C conflates two distinct mechanisms; D denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The system occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking answers that, on manual review, misstate a specific holding from the correctly retrieved opinion.

choices.text: Apply defensive validation — check extracted holdings against the actual source excerpt rather than trusting confident phrasing.
Trust the fluent, well-cited-looking output as sufficient evidence that the holding was already validated.
Say this is purely a model limitation with no architectural mitigation available at all.
Increase the output's length, on the theory that more room to elaborate reduces misstatement risk.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted holdings against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. B is the failure mode itself; D doesn't address correctness; C incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether attorney-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection for the research platform.

choices.text: Say latency should never factor into model or architecture decisions, regardless of the platform's SLA.
Say only cost should factor into tier selection, and latency should never be part of that decision.
Weigh accuracy needs against the latency and cost the SLA can tolerate, instead of defaulting to the most capable tier regardless of SLA.
Treat SLAs as a stakeholder-communication topic with no bearing on the technical tier-selection decision.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, B, and D each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The platform currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Pin the current production version and evaluate the new release against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading.
Keep floating to "latest" automatically in production, since a newer model is always better than an older one.
Never upgrade the model again once an initial version has been chosen for production.
Upgrade immediately without testing, since an improved benchmark score guarantees a production improvement.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. B and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; C over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: RAG Integration for a Legal Case-Law Research Platform
questions.scenario_context: Caselight is a legal research platform that wants Claude to answer attorney questions using retrieval over case law, statutes, and secondary treatises, combined with general reasoning. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer.
questions.prompt: The platform's context budget is a concern because both the system prompt/citation rules and the retrieved case excerpts must fit alongside room for a detailed analytical answer.

choices.text: Treat input and output token budgets as entirely independent of one another within a single context window.
Say this tradeoff only matters for unusually long documents that approach the model's maximum context window, never for a typical query.
Say output length has no practical limit, regardless of how much retrieved content the input already uses.
Balance retrieved-content volume against room for a detailed answer, since input and output share one context budget.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and C all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.
