questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Discovery reveals the client's actual goal is reducing average escalation resolution time by unifying the three disconnected queues, at the same staffing level — not adding new self-service capabilities customers currently lack.

choices.text: Frame the architecture around efficiency, building resolution-time and handle-volume metrics rather than novel-capability claims.
Frame it around transformation instead, since collapsing three queues into one is inherently a transformational change no matter what discovery found.
Frame it around cost reduction only, on the assumption that staffing cost is always the real driver behind a queue-consolidation project like this.
Skip picking a specific value pillar entirely — a system that measurably works speaks for itself regardless of how the business frames its goals.

questions.explanation: A goal of more volume/consistency within the same staffing and cycle time is a throughput/efficiency problem; naming that pillar correctly shapes both architecture and success metrics. B, C, and D either misname the pillar or skip the framing discovery actually surfaced.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Escalation handling requires different steps depending on the issue category, customer tier, and information uncovered mid-conversation (for example, discovering a device is under an active recall).

choices.text: A fixed workflow, since escalations of this kind always follow the same script no matter what the customer says mid-call.
An agentic pattern, since the right sequence of steps varies by case and depends on findings uncovered mid-conversation.
An augmented LLM pattern, since one retrieval-enhanced call is always treated as sufficient regardless of how the case actually unfolds.
Whichever pattern prototypes fastest, since fixed workflows, agentic patterns, and augmented calls are functionally interchangeable here.

questions.explanation: Steps that vary by case and depend on intermediate findings are the defining case for an agentic pattern. A assumes a predictability the scenario lacks; C undersells the orchestration needed; D ignores that the patterns have real, non-interchangeable tradeoffs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The proposed design uses a coordinator agent delegating to specialized subagents (billing-dispute, device-warranty, network-outage-diagnostics, retention-offer).

choices.text: Let each subagent message whichever subagent needs its output next directly, skipping the coordinator entirely to minimize hops.
Merge all four responsibilities and their entire toolsets into a single subagent, trading specialization for less coordination overhead and simpler routing logic.
Let subagents talk to each other directly, but log the traffic afterward so the coordinator can review it during a later audit.
Route inter-subagent traffic through the coordinator to preserve observability, error handling, and controlled information flow.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. A and C sacrifice these properties for a shortcut; B discards the specialization that motivated separate subagents.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Every subagent completes its assigned work correctly, but the coordinator's decomposition routes billing, device, and network escalations correctly while retention-eligible cases (customers actively threatening to cancel) are never routed to any subagent and silently fall through.

choices.text: Add a fifth, generic catch-all subagent whose only job is to absorb whatever escalation type the other four don't recognize as their own.
Give the existing subagents broader tool access, on the reasoning that any one of them could, in principle, be stretched to handle any escalation type.
Fix the coordinator's decomposition so it explicitly covers retention-eligible cases, instead of tuning the subagents that already work.
Add a prompt instruction telling every subagent to flag any escalation it personally doesn't recognize as its own to handle.

questions.explanation: Every subagent succeeding while an entire escalation category is never routed at all is a decomposition problem at the coordinator level, not a subagent performance problem. A, B, and D all patch downstream instead of fixing the actual scope gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The design must align technical architecture to a specific business value pillar Meridian actually cares about, distinct from a generic "we added AI" narrative.

choices.text: Any AI system inherently demonstrates transformation on its own, so no additional framing work is needed from the architect.
Efficiency, transformation, cost, and performance SLAs are example pillars; the chosen one should drive both architecture and metrics.
Treat business value pillars as a sales-team concern that the architecture itself doesn't need to reference at all, regardless of what discovery surfaced.
Choose the pillar after the system ships, based on whichever benefit turns out easiest to measure in hindsight, rather than up front.

questions.explanation: Business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs) give both the architecture and its metrics a clear anchor. A, C, and D all skip or defer this framing in ways that risk building toward the wrong measure of success.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: Frontline escalation agents are skeptical of the new system and worried it will be used to justify headcount reductions; discovery interviews surface this repeatedly.

choices.text: Ignore the sentiment entirely in the discussion, treating adoption concerns as something only change management should handle.
Treat it as a real implicit constraint shaping adoption and rollout sequencing, alongside the explicit technical requirements raised in discovery.
Proceed with the technical design and hand the sentiment entirely to change management, with no architectural input either way at all.
Recommend against the project outright, based on the sentiment alone and independent of the technical case for it entirely.

questions.explanation: Adoption sentiment is a real implicit constraint that should shape rollout sequencing and where human-in-the-loop checkpoints matter — it's discovery input, not noise to ignore. A and C treat it as out of scope; D overreacts to sentiment alone without weighing it against the technical case.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why the network-outage-diagnostics subagent uses a higher-capability, higher-cost model tier than the billing-dispute subagent.

choices.text: Use the same tier everywhere for simplicity, regardless of how much reasoning depth each task actually needs.
Answer that a higher tier is used because outage work is simply "more important," without giving any further technical detail.
Avoid explaining the tier difference at all, on the assumption that stakeholders don't need or want technical detail.
Explain the tradeoff: outage diagnostics needs deeper telemetry reasoning, while billing disputes are simpler and cheaper to serve.

questions.explanation: Explaining the specific tradeoff (deeper reasoning need vs. added cost/latency) is the standard for stakeholder communication about architectural decisions. A and B withhold the reasoning stakeholders need; C removes a deliberate, justified difference for false simplicity.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The architecture's current design produces a final retention-offer recommendation with no mechanism to learn from which offers customers actually accepted or rejected over time.

choices.text: Treat this as acceptable, since the initial design was validated at launch and already reflects best practice.
Treat feedback loops as a data-science concern that sits entirely outside the architecture, with no hooks needed in the system design.
Add a feedback loop capturing offer acceptance and rejection outcomes as a first-class architectural hook.
Defer any feedback mechanism to a hypothetical future phase, with no hooks for it in the current design.

questions.explanation: Adding a feedback loop that captures offer outcomes as a first-class architectural component is what lets the system improve after deployment. A, B, and D all treat a first-class architectural component as optional or someone else's problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The client wants a single enhanced LLM call — with retrieval of the customer's plan and billing history — to answer straightforward "why is my bill higher this month" questions, without any multi-step autonomous orchestration.

choices.text: Build a full multi-agent architecture regardless of the task's simplicity, rewriting the system prompt for orchestration it doesn't need.
Conclude this cannot be built with Claude at all, on the reasoning that it isn't structured as a multi-step autonomous agent.
Require a structured fixed workflow with at least five sequential steps, regardless of how simple the underlying billing question actually is.
Use an augmented LLM pattern — a single call enhanced with retrieval — fitting this simpler need without agentic orchestration overhead.

questions.explanation: A single call enhanced with retrieval, without multi-step autonomous orchestration, is exactly what an augmented LLM pattern is for. A and C over-engineer a simple augmentation need; B is factually wrong.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The billing-dispute subagent's toolset has grown to include tools for tasks like device-shipping tracking and network-status lookups that are unrelated to billing disputes.

choices.text: Remove or relocate the unrelated tools, since capability bloat degrades tool-selection reliability.
Treat this as having no architectural downside, as long as the subagent's prompt is well-written enough to compensate.
Treat more tools as always improving a subagent's flexibility, and encourage adding still more over time.
Increase the subagent's context window instead, on the theory that a bigger window will fully offset the added tool count and keep selection reliable.

questions.explanation: Tools unrelated to a subagent's core role degrade tool-selection reliability as the candidate set grows — the fix is removing or relocating them, not writing around it. B and C ignore this real degradation; D doesn't address selection reliability at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Multi-Agent Customer-Escalation Platform for a Telecom Retailer
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Mobile, a regional telecom retailer, wants to modernize how it handles customer escalations that arrive through three previously disconnected queues — billing disputes, device warranty claims, and network outage complaints — plus a fourth workflow for retention offers to at-risk subscribers. You are the architect responsible for the end-to-end design, including whether and how to use a multi-agent pattern, and for running discovery with Meridian's stakeholders.
questions.prompt: The coordinator currently processes each escalation sequentially through billing-dispute lookup, device-warranty lookup, and retention-offer scoring, even though device-warranty lookup and retention-offer scoring have no dependency on each other's output.

choices.text: Combine device-warranty lookup and retention-offer scoring into one subagent, so the sequencing question never has to be answered.
Run device-warranty lookup and retention-offer scoring as independent, parallel calls once billing-dispute lookup completes.
Treat sequential processing as required for auditability, regardless of whether the steps actually depend on each other.
Treat parallelization as impossible within a coordinator/subagent architecture in general, regardless of whether steps share any real dependency.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent calls with no data dependency between them can run in parallel once their shared prerequisite completes, reducing latency without sacrificing correctness. A and C misstate real constraints; D avoids the sequencing question rather than answering it.

choices.text: Present only the model names and per-call token costs involved, leaving the actual escalation flow undescribed for the committee.
Describe input, processing, output, and the feedback loop at a level the committee can evaluate against business outcomes.
Present the full technical architecture diagram, including every subagent's internal prompt and tool schema, without any simplification for a non-technical audience.
Skip a high-level description entirely and go straight into a live implementation demo of the coordinator and subagents.

questions.explanation: A steering committee needs the architecture communicated at the level of business-outcome evaluation, not implementation internals. A is insufficient detail; C is too much of the wrong kind of detail; D skips the communication need entirely.

choices.text: A single agent holding every tool is more likely to suffer degraded tool-selection reliability than specialized subagents.
A single generalist agent scales better as tool count grows, since it avoids maintaining separate subagent boundaries.
Treat specialized subagents as strictly a cost-increasing choice, with no reliability benefit to offset the added complexity.
Treat the two approaches as architecturally equivalent, with no meaningful reliability or cost difference between a generalist agent and specialized subagents.

questions.explanation: A single generalist agent holding every tool and responsibility is more exposed to degraded tool-selection reliability than agents scoped to narrower roles — the core argument for specialization. B, C, and D all understate or deny this real architectural tradeoff.

choices.text: Build full support for streaming-bundle disputes now, filling in the missing requirements with reasonable-sounding guesses.
Ignore future escalation categories entirely until concrete requirements exist for them, even ones already announced as coming next year.
Refuse to proceed with the current phase of work until every future requirement is fully finalized and signed off by stakeholders.
Design the current decomposition with reasonable extensibility in mind, without over-building for speculative, undefined requirements down the line.

questions.explanation: Reasonable extensibility without over-building for undefined future requirements balances current delivery against future flexibility. A wastes effort guessing at undefined requirements; B ignores a known future need entirely; C blocks current delivery unnecessarily.

Plan around the original architect remaining available indefinitely on call, instead of investing in documentation now.
Document the reasoning behind key decisions — pattern choices, decomposition, tier selections — not just the final configuration values.
Treat documentation as unnecessary, on the assumption that clean, well-organized code already makes the reasoning self-evident.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: Most buyer questions to the copilot are moderately complex; a small fraction require deep multi-step reasoning across many SKUs and vendors, and a small fraction are simple lookups (for example, "current on-hand units for SKU 4471").

choices.text: Route by task difficulty: a fast tier for lookups, a balanced tier for typical questions, and a higher tier for deep multi-step cases.
Use the highest-capability tier on every question, to guarantee quality regardless of how simple the underlying lookup is.
Use one fixed model tier for every question, treating complexity as irrelevant to tier selection, since routing logic adds engineering overhead the team would rather avoid.
Use the fastest tier on every question to minimize cost, accepting the resulting quality loss on the harder cases.

questions.explanation: Routing by task difficulty matches the fast/balanced/high-capability tiers to the actual mix of simple, typical, and complex questions. B and D sacrifice fit-to-task or quality; C ignores complexity variation entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: Every request to the copilot sends the same long system prompt (merchandiser persona, formatting rules, category taxonomy) followed by retrieved SKU and vendor data that varies per query.

choices.text: Put the retrieved content first, on the reasoning that it's the part most relevant to the specific query being asked.
Place the stable system prompt first and enable caching, with retrieved content after it, to reduce latency and cost.
Alternate system instructions and retrieved content throughout the prompt so both stay close to whatever they relate to.
Treat prompt ordering as having no effect on cost or latency for a use case like this one, even at high query volume with heavy caching potential.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled, and variable content after, maximizes the cacheable prefix across high query volume, reducing latency and cost. A, C, and D all misstate or break the caching opportunity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: The merchandising corpus mixes long-form vendor contracts and category strategy memos with short structured data (a table of weekly sell-through by SKU).

choices.text: Use the largest possible chunk size for everything, skipping schema- or shape-specific tuning, on the theory that one large-chunk strategy is simplest to build and maintain long-term.
Assume one chunking and indexing strategy tuned for long-form documents can serve both content types equally well.
Match chunking and indexing strategy to each data shape — long-form documents need different chunking than short structured records.
Exclude the structured sell-through data from retrieval entirely, relying only on the long-form documents.

questions.explanation: Chunking and indexing strategy must match each data shape; a single strategy tuned for one content type degrades retrieval for the mismatched type. A and B ignore this mismatch; D discards useful structured data.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: Buyer queries range from exact lookups ("current inventory for SKU 4471") to conceptual questions ("how has the athleisure category's margin story evolved this year").

choices.text: Use only embedding similarity search for every query type, regardless of whether the query is an exact lookup.
Match retrieval strategy to query pattern — metadata filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where both are needed.
Use only structured metadata filtering for every query type, including the open-ended conceptual ones.

Treat query pattern as entirely irrelevant to which retrieval approach is appropriate, since a single, well-tuned embedding index should already generalize across every kind of query without further tailoring.

questions.explanation: Matching retrieval mechanism to query pattern — structured filtering for exact lookups, embeddings for conceptual questions, hybrid where needed — is the correct architecture. A and C force one mechanism onto queries it doesn't fit; D denies a real, consequential distinction.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: Buyers need each margin or forecast claim reliably mapped to a specific source document and section, and generic prose responses often lose this mapping.

choices.text: Ask the model, in prose, to "always cite sources" without any further structure or output validation behind it.
Add citations after generation by searching for a plausible-looking source for each claim already produced, matching phrasing rather than verifying the underlying figure.
Require structured output pairing each claim with its source (document, section, excerpt) so citation mapping survives synthesis.
Append a general bibliography of consulted documents at the end of each response, without linking individual claims to it.

questions.explanation: Structured claim-source pairing preserves citation mapping through synthesis; prose citation requests and after-the-fact citation search are exactly the patterns that lose or fabricate mappings. A, B, and D all reintroduce the failure mode the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: Two retrieved sources disagree on a vendor's quoted unit cost by a small margin — likely because one reflects a pre-rebate price and the other a post-rebate net price.

choices.text: Average the two figures together and present the average as the unit cost, treating the discrepancy as noise rather than a real methodological difference.
Prefer whichever source was retrieved first, regardless of which figure it happens to contain or how the two prices were actually calculated.
Present both figures explicitly, annotated as a discrepancy, with source attribution and the likely methodological explanation.
Omit the unit cost figure from the response entirely, since the two sources disagree and no single number can be confidently reported.

questions.explanation: Presenting both figures with attribution and a likely methodological explanation preserves the actual information for the buyer rather than resolving a real discrepancy arbitrarily. A, B, and D all discard or obscure a genuine data conflict.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: A prompt asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with source fields" still occasionally produces a conversational preamble before the JSON.

choices.text: Use tool-use or schema-constrained output so structure is enforced by the API mechanism, not by adjusting temperature.
Repeat the same instruction more emphatically, in stronger language, elsewhere in the prompt.
Post-process every response to strip any leading text that appears before the first `{`.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's room for both the preamble and the JSON to fit, plus extra buffer in case the model adds trailing commentary after the closing brace too.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests or sampling-parameter tweaks that can still drift. B and C are workarounds for a structurally solvable problem; D doesn't address the preamble at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: The copilot needs to connect to a proprietary internal vendor-catalog system, exposing search and lookup capabilities to multiple other internal Claude-powered tools beyond just the merchandising copilot.

choices.text: Hard-code the vendor-catalog integration directly into this one copilot's application code, with no reuse path for other tools.
Paste the entire vendor catalog into every prompt sent to every consuming tool, refreshing the pasted copy manually whenever the catalog changes upstream.
Build an MCP server exposing the vendor-catalog operations as tools and resources, reusable across the internal tools that need it.
Require each consuming tool to reimplement its own vendor-catalog integration independently, from scratch.

questions.explanation: An MCP server matches the described need: reusable access across multiple different internal Claude-powered tools, maintained independently. A, B, and D all fail the reuse or maintainability requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding between exposing the full vendor catalog directly in every prompt versus letting the agent query a catalog resource only when needed.

choices.text: Treat loading the full catalog up front as always preferable, since completeness matters more than context cost, latency, or how much the catalog is expected to grow.
Treat the two approaches as having no meaningful difference in context cost between them.
Refuse to expose the catalog to the agent in any form, forcing all lookups through a human intermediary.
Use progressive discovery — querying a catalog resource as needed — scaling better than loading the entire catalog up front.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery via a queryable catalog resource scales with catalog growth better than loading the entire catalog into every prompt. A and B ignore the real context cost of the monolithic approach; C removes needed capability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: A buyer asks a chain-of-thought-friendly question requiring the model to reason step by step across several vendor contracts and sell-through reports before recommending a reorder quantity.

choices.text: Use zero-shot prompting with no reasoning guidance, treating it as always equally effective regardless of task structure.
Treat multi-document reasoning as something the model cannot do at all, regardless of prompting approach or how the reasoning steps are structured.
Use a chain-of-thought approach, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, suited to this multi-document synthesis question.
Restrict chain-of-thought prompting to coding tasks only, on the assumption it doesn't transfer to document synthesis.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting, allowing explicit intermediate reasoning, fits multi-document synthesis requiring step-by-step reasoning. A, B, and D all misstate the fit or capability of prompting techniques for this task.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: The copilot wants to standardize prompt fragments (citation format, category taxonomy, formatting rules) across several different buyer-facing features so changes propagate consistently.

choices.text: Duplicate the fragments into each feature's own structured prompt independently, updating each copy by hand.
Treat modular prompt fragments as the same mechanism as prompt caching, and rely on caching alone to keep them consistent.

Treat standardization across features as unachievable through prompt design, since only a single shared system prompt could keep them consistent, and even that doesn't scale well across many features.
Use modular, composable, versioned prompt fragments shared across features — distinct from caching (a cost/latency lever) or Skills (a capability lever).

questions.explanation: Modular, versioned prompt fragments are a maintainability lever distinct from caching (cost/latency) and Skills (capability packaging) — the right tool for consistent propagation of shared fragments across features. A reintroduces duplication; B conflates two distinct mechanisms; C denies a real, common architecture pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: The copilot occasionally returns confident, well-cited-looking margin figures that, on manual review, misstate a specific number from the correctly retrieved source report.

choices.text: Trust the fluent, well-formatted output as evidence that the cited figure is correct, since citation formatting alone signals accuracy.
Increase output length, on the reasoning that more room in the response leaves more space for the model to work out and double-check the correct figure.
Apply defensive validation, verifying extracted figures against the source excerpt rather than trusting confident phrasing.
Treat this as purely a model limitation with no architectural mitigation available, regardless of what verification steps might catch it.

questions.explanation: Verifying extracted figures against source excerpts catches confident-but-wrong output that fluent formatting alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; B doesn't address correctness; D incorrectly claims no architectural mitigation exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: The team debates whether buyer-facing latency SLAs should factor into model tier selection for the merchandising copilot.

choices.text: Let only cost factor into tier selection, treating latency as irrelevant to the decision.
Treat SLAs as a stakeholder-communication concern only, with no bearing on technical architecture or model tier selection decisions at all.
Treat latency as something that should never factor into model or architecture decisions.
Weigh accuracy against the SLA's latency and cost tolerance, rather than defaulting to peak capability.

questions.explanation: Weighing accuracy needs against latency/cost relative to the SLA is standard model-tier decision-making; defaulting to maximum capability regardless of SLA ignores a real, decidable tradeoff. A, B, and C each drop a relevant factor from the decision.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Model Selection and Context Engineering for a Retail Merchandising Copilot
questions.scenario_context: Harborview Retail Group, a multi-category apparel retailer, wants Claude to help category buyers answer questions using both general reasoning and retrieval over a large, constantly-updated corpus of vendor contracts, sell-through reports, and category strategy memos. You're architecting the model selection, prompting approach, and integration layer for the merchandising copilot.
questions.prompt: A new model version is released with improved benchmark scores. The merchandising copilot currently floats to "latest" automatically in production.

choices.text: Continue floating to latest automatically, on the reasoning that newer benchmark scores are validation enough on their own, regardless of behavioral drift risk.
Never upgrade models once the initial version is chosen, treating current behavior as permanently fixed and deterministic.
Pin the current version in production and evaluate the new version against the platform's own tests before deliberately upgrading.
Upgrade immediately without testing, on the assumption that benchmark improvements guarantee production improvements.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing against the platform's own evaluation before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift, even when benchmark scores improve. A and D assume benchmark gains transfer automatically; B over-corrects into permanent stagnation.

choices.text: Treat input and output token budgets as entirely independent, so schema design or content volume on one side never affects headroom on the other.
Treat this tradeoff as only mattering for unusually long documents, never for typical queries.
Treat output length as having no practical limit, regardless of how much input content is already in context.
Input and output share one context-window budget, so retrieved content must be balanced against room for a detailed answer.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, directly constraining how much retrieved content and answer detail can coexist. A, B, and C all misstate this real, architecture-relevant constraint.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team currently measures only technician first-time-fix rate and hasn't defined targets for latency, cost, or safety.

choices.text: Treat latency and cost as operations concerns that sit outside evaluation design entirely.
Define metrics spanning accuracy, latency, cost, and safety as first-class alongside first-time-fix rate.
Treat first-time-fix rate alone as sufficient, since it's the system's primary stated purpose and the only metric leadership originally asked to track.
Treat safety metrics as relevant only for explicitly regulated industries.

questions.explanation: Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety/security should all be defined as first-class metrics, since a system failing on any of them fails overall even if first-time-fix rate improves. A, C, and D each drop a dimension that materially affects whether the system is actually working well.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The evaluation dataset currently consists only of automated accuracy checks against a fixed labeled set of past dispatch tickets.

choices.text: Treat a single automated method as sufficient for any production system, regardless of what edge cases or safety-relevant paths it fails to cover.
Replace the automated checks entirely with human review as the sole evaluation method going forward.
Expand the labeled set indefinitely, treating dataset size as the only improvement lever available.
Use mixed methodologies — automated eval, human review, and adversarial testing — since no single method covers every failure mode.

questions.explanation: Mixed methodologies (automated, human, adversarial) are needed because no single method covers every failure mode, especially safety-relevant edge cases. A, B, and C each over-rely on or discard one method without addressing the actual coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to test whether a new prompt version improves technician-recommendation quality before rolling it out to all dispatch traffic.

choices.text: Roll the new prompt out to all traffic immediately, watching for problems only after the fact instead of testing beforehand at all.
Change the prompt and the model tier at the same time, assuming deterministic output will make attribution easy afterward, even with two variables changing together.
Skip testing altogether, treating prompt changes as inherently low-risk regardless of how technician-facing recommendations might change.
Run an A/B test changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline, so any difference can be attributed to that change.

questions.explanation: Changing only the prompt version against a stable baseline is what allows the observed difference to be attributed correctly to that one change. A skips testing entirely; B confounds two variables; C dismisses a real risk without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: A dispatch recommendation cites the wrong required part number. Investigation shows the underlying parts-catalog lookup returned correct, current data, and the model's response paraphrased it inaccurately.

choices.text: Treat this as a prompt/generation issue, calling for prompt or output-validation fixes rather than retrieval changes.
Treat this as a retrieval problem and fix the indexing pipeline instead, even though the pipeline already returned correct, current data.
Treat this as impossible to diagnose without a full model retraining cycle, regardless of what the paraphrasing error actually indicates.
Treat this as a model-tier mismatch requiring a different, higher tier, regardless of what the investigation actually found about where the error occurred.

questions.explanation: Correct retrieval plus inaccurate paraphrasing is a generation-side issue, calling for prompt/output-validation fixes rather than retrieval or model-tier changes. B and D misdiagnose the layer at fault; C avoids diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Immediately after a scheduled parts-catalog refresh, the dispatch assistant starts recommending obsolete part numbers, while model version and average latency are unchanged.

choices.text: Suspect a temperature setting change, since the assistant's apparent confidence changed, even though no temperature parameter was actually touched in the refresh.
Suspect the model was silently updated by the provider, despite the version string staying the same.
Investigate the retrieval and indexing layer first, since the regression tracks the data refresh event with model and latency unchanged.
Suspect the context window shrank, rather than the structured retrieval layer that was just refreshed.

questions.explanation: A regression tied specifically to a data refresh event, with model and latency unchanged, points first at retrieval/indexing. A, B, and D would not specifically correlate with a parts-catalog refresh.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to reduce cost and latency for dispatch recommendations but is worried about hurting first-time-fix accuracy, and currently has no data on where the current configuration sits on that tradeoff curve.

choices.text: Optimize cost, latency, and accuracy jointly against the system's actual SLA and budget, not any single dimension in isolation.
Maximize accuracy without regard to cost or latency, treating a slower, pricier configuration as always the safer choice.
Optimize cost, latency, and accuracy independently of each other, treating each as a fixed, deterministic target on its own.
Treat this tradeoff as unmeasurable, something that can only be guessed at rather than tested.

questions.explanation: Joint optimization against the actual SLA and budget avoids both an unsustainably expensive "accuracy at all costs" outcome and a cheap configuration that fails the accuracy bar. B and C optimize dimensions in isolation; D claims the tradeoff is unmeasurable when it is not.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Production monitoring for the dispatch assistant currently reports only an overall weekly average accuracy score.

choices.text: Treat a single aggregate average, once validated, as sufficient for production monitoring regardless of segment performance.
Have monitoring surface drift and outliers — a per-specialty breakdown — since an aggregate average can hide a failing segment.
Treat weekly granularity as always sufficient, regardless of how the system is actually behaving across specialties.
Have monitoring track only cost, on the assumption that accuracy is already fully captured by the eval suite alone.

questions.explanation: Segment/outlier-aware monitoring surfaces problems an aggregate weekly average can hide. A and C accept a monitoring blind spot; D drops accuracy monitoring from observability entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team proposes cutting human review of flagged low-confidence dispatch recommendations by 80%, citing a 96% aggregate accuracy score.

choices.text: Segment accuracy by issue type and specialty before cutting review, since an aggregate figure can mask a failing segment.
Proceed with the review cut based on the 96% aggregate figure alone, without further segmentation.
Treat aggregate accuracy as definitionally representative of every individual segment.
Treat human review as something that should never be reduced, regardless of measured accuracy, segment performance, or the actual cost of maintaining it.

questions.explanation: Segmenting accuracy by issue type and technician specialty before cutting review protects against a failing segment hiding behind a healthy aggregate. B and C trust the aggregate uncritically; D over-corrects by refusing any reduction regardless of evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An A/B test shows a new prompt version improves first-time-fix rate, but the team has not checked whether it also changed the rate of recommending an on-site visit for issues that should have been resolved remotely.

choices.text: Treat first-time-fix rate alone as a sufficient signal to ship the change without checking any other dispatch-outcome metric.
Check the remote-resolution-eligible failure mode before shipping, since a fix-rate gain could increase unnecessary dispatches unnoticed.
Treat this failure mode as something evaluation is structurally unable to measure, no matter how the test data or dispatch logs are instrumented.
Ship the change and monitor informally afterward, in place of testing for this specific failure mode beforehand.

questions.explanation: An isolated first-time-fix improvement could mask a worsened dispatch-necessity failure mode; checking specifically for that before shipping is the correct diagnostic step. A and D ship without adequate testing; C incorrectly claims the failure mode is unmeasurable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to diagnose why a subset of technically accurate dispatch recommendations are rated poorly by technicians in post-job surveys.

choices.text: Investigate a dimension beyond accuracy, like clarity or field practicality, since "accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured gap.
Assume the accuracy metric itself is broken and discard it outright, without checking any other explanation for the low ratings first.
Increase the model's capability tier, assuming higher capability always improves structured output ratings regardless of what technicians are actually reacting to.
Ignore technician satisfaction scores entirely, in favor of the accuracy metric alone, since surveys are harder to standardize than an automated check.

questions.explanation: "Accurate but poorly rated" points at an unmeasured quality dimension (clarity, completeness, practicality) rather than a broken accuracy metric. B and D discard a working, differently-scoped metric; C assumes a fix without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team is optimizing token usage and notices the system sends the full ticket history plus a large static equipment-manual excerpt on every turn of multi-turn dispatch conversations.

choices.text: Treat this as having no optimization opportunity, on the assumption that full history is always required on every turn.
Remove the equipment-manual excerpt entirely, without an alternative source for the content it provided to technicians.
Switch to a smaller model as the only lever for reducing token cost, even though redundant static content is the larger driver.
Apply prompt caching to the static equipment-manual excerpt, and trim or summarize older ticket-history turns to cut token cost.

questions.explanation: Caching the static equipment-manual excerpt and trimming/summarizing older turns directly reduces redundant token cost in multi-turn conversations. A denies an obvious lever; B removes needed content; C is a blunt, quality-risking lever when a more targeted fix is available.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Logging captures every raw prompt and response for the dispatch assistant, and the team treats this as their observability strategy, but no one can identify emerging failure patterns from the volume of raw logs.

choices.text: Treat raw logging at full volume, by itself, as a sufficient and complete observability strategy for any production system regardless of scale.
Reduce logging volume to save storage cost, treating that as a full fix even though the signals stay unstructured and unreviewable.
Treat observability as requiring no structure at all, as long as every prompt and response is retained somewhere on disk indefinitely.
Redesign observability toward structured, aggregable signals — sampling, tagged categories, segment metrics — since raw logs aren't reviewable at volume.

questions.explanation: Structured, sampled, and tagged signals are what make observability actionable at volume; raw logs alone aren't reviewable. A and C accept the described dysfunction; B addresses cost, not the actual observability gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: The team wants to identify whether a recent quality regression was caused by a prompt change, a model version change, or an equipment-manual content update — all three happened in the same week.

choices.text: Assume whichever change shipped most recently is automatically the cause, without checking the other two changes at all.
Revert all three changes without investigation, regardless of which one, if any, actually caused the regression, and regardless of the cost of reverting each.
Treat attribution as impossible once multiple changes ship in the same week, even though each one could still be tested in isolation afterward.
This is why changes should ship one variable at a time — with three at once, attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently.

questions.explanation: With three simultaneous changes, correct attribution requires isolating and re-testing each independently — exactly the discipline one-variable-at-a-time testing is meant to preserve. A and B guess without evidence; C gives up on a solvable (if effortful) diagnostic problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: An automated eval asserts that a dispatch-summary output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even on outputs a human reviewer would call correct.

choices.text: Make the reference string longer, on the assumption that added length will resolve the intermittent failures.
Conclude the model is malfunctioning and needs retraining, since its outputs can no longer be validated against the fixed string.
Increase the temperature setting to fix the intermittent failures, on the reasoning that more randomness will somehow stabilize matching.
Exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool for non-deterministic LLM output; the eval should check content and structure, not exact text.

questions.explanation: Non-deterministic output makes exact-string-match evals structurally unsuited to this task; content/structure-based checks are the correct fix. B and C misdiagnose model behavior as broken; A doesn't address the actual mismatch between eval design and output variability.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Evaluation and Monitoring of a Field-Service Dispatch Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Atlas Utilities operates a fleet of field-service technicians who service gas and electric meters. A Claude-powered dispatch assistant recommends likely fault causes, required parts, and whether an issue can be resolved remotely versus requiring an on-site visit. It's been in production for several months, and you're responsible for the evaluation strategy, diagnosing quality issues, and optimizing cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single number to represent "how good" the dispatch assistant is, to track over time.

choices.text: Treat a single number as always achievable and sufficient on its own, regardless of how many dimensions quality actually spans.
Use first-time-fix rate alone as that single number, since it's the system's stated purpose and the metric leadership already recognizes.
Offer a single aggregate metric as a top-line indicator, but pair it with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a failing area.
Refuse to provide any single summary metric, under any circumstances leadership might reasonably ask for one to track.

questions.explanation: A top-line number can be useful communication but should be paired with segment- and dimension-level detail so it doesn't mask a specific failing area. A and B oversimplify to a single lossy number; D refuses a reasonable, common stakeholder request.
